## Core difference

**jsdom simulates browser APIs inside Node.js; Browser Mode runs tests in a real browser.** Vitest describes jsdom as a partially implemented browser environment, whereas Browser Mode runs unit or integration tests without mocking that environment. [Comparisons](https://vitest.dev/guide/comparisons.html) · [Environment configuration](https://vitest.dev/config/environment.html)

## What changes for component tests?

| Area | jsdom | Browser Mode |
|---|---|---|
| Rendering and layout | Does not perform real layout; layout-dependent properties such as `offsetTop` are limited. | Exercises actual browser layout and styling. |
| Browser APIs | Some APIs are missing, including the documented example `window.navigation`. | Uses the browser’s native implementations. |
| Interactions | Simulated behavior can miss browser-specific issues. | Tests real event propagation, focus, scrolling, and related accessibility behavior. |

These are key reasons Vitest recommends Browser Mode for component testing. [Comparisons](https://vitest.dev/guide/comparisons.html) · [Component testing](https://vitest.dev/guide/browser/component-testing)

## Setup and testing APIs

- **jsdom:** Select it using `--environment=jsdom` or a per-file `@vitest-environment jsdom` comment. Vitest also exposes the current instance through a `jsdom` global; TypeScript users can include `vitest/jsdom` types. [Environment configuration](https://vitest.dev/config/environment.html)
- **Browser Mode:** Requires starting a browser provider and browser instance. Component examples use browser locators such as `page.getByRole()`, awaited interactions such as `.click()` and `.fill()`, and auto-retrying assertions such as `await expect.element(...).toBeInTheDocument()`. Existing Testing Library rendering can be bridged through `page.elementLocator(baseElement)`. [Why Browser Mode](https://main.vitest.dev/guide/browser/why.html) · [Component testing](https://vitest.dev/guide/browser/component-testing)
- **Network mocking:** The component guide uses MSW’s browser-side `setupWorker` for Browser Mode, rather than the Node-side `setupServer` used with jsdom. [Component testing](https://vitest.dev/guide/browser/component-testing)

## Trade-offs and limitations

Browser Mode has **longer initialization**, because it must start the provider and browser. jsdom remains useful for fast, headless tests that need DOM APIs but not real rendering. Browser Mode is also **not a replacement for a complete end-to-end testing tool**; Vitest recommends complementing it with a standalone browser runner. [Why Browser Mode](https://main.vitest.dev/guide/browser/why.html) · [Comparisons](https://vitest.dev/guide/comparisons.html)

**Evidence gap:** The four retrieved pages did not provide the complete Browser Mode configuration or limitations reference. Exact provider installation, CI requirements, and a comprehensive compatibility list therefore remain unverified here.

## Presence is separate from a field’s value

In proto3, these declarations behave differently:

```proto
int32 count = 1;           // implicit presence
optional int32 limit = 2;  // explicit presence
```

- **Implicit presence:** the generated API stores the value but does not distinguish “never set” from “set to the default.”
- **Explicit presence (`optional`):** the API also tracks whether the field was set—even when its value is the default.

Protobuf recommends using `optional` for proto3 basic types. Singular message fields already track presence; adding `optional` does not change their behavior. [Field Presence](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/field_presence/), [Proto3 Guide](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/proto3/)

## Default values and generated APIs

Unset scalar fields read as their type’s default: numeric types return zero, booleans return `false`, strings return `""`, and bytes return an empty value. An unset `optional` scalar returns the same default, **but presence remains separately observable**. [Proto3 Guide](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/proto3/)

With explicit presence, generated APIs provide presence-checking and clearing operations—for example, `has_foo()` and `clear_foo()` in APIs using that naming convention. Setting an optional field to zero makes it **present**; clearing it makes it **absent**. Exact method names vary by language. Implicit-presence scalar APIs generally lack a presence check; the documentation notes Dart as an exception. [Field Presence](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/field_presence/)

## What happens on the wire?

| Field state | Implicit presence | Explicit presence |
|---|---|---|
| Unset | Omitted | Omitted |
| Set to default | Omitted | Serialized |
| Set to non-default | Serialized | Serialized |

Thus, `optional` changes how generated APIs retain presence and decide what to serialize—not the basic encoding of the field’s value. Empty strings can exist as present values in wire data, but an implicit-presence API may discard that distinction when reserializing. [Field Presence](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/field_presence/)

For example, a sender using `optional int32 foo` can serialize an explicitly set `foo = 0`. A receiver using implicit-presence `int32 foo` reads zero but omits it when reserializing. The original sender then reads the returned field as absent. The schemas are wire-compatible, but the round trip loses presence information. [Field Presence](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/field_presence/)

## Merging consequence

Implicit-presence merging skips default-valued fields, so a patch cannot express “set this value to zero” through ordinary merging alone; an external mechanism such as `FieldMask` is needed. Explicit presence allows a present default value to be merged. [Field Presence](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/field_presence/)

**Scope:** This describes general protobuf semantics; language-specific accessor spelling and implementation details require the relevant generated-code guide.

## 1. Row-level security (RLS)

RLS is PostgreSQL’s mechanism for deciding **which rows a role may read or change**. Table privileges determine whether an operation is allowed at all; RLS then restricts its rows. Enable RLS and define policies with SQL, for example:

```sql
alter table public.todos enable row level security;

create policy "Read own todos"
on public.todos for select
to authenticated
using ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);
```

This effectively adds a user-specific filter to reads. `USING` controls access to existing rows; `WITH CHECK` validates inserted or updated rows. Updates generally need both clauses and a corresponding SELECT policy. With RLS enabled and no applicable policies, client API access is denied. [RLS documentation](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security)

Unauthenticated requests use `anon`; signed-in users use `authenticated`. Supabase Auth’s anonymous sign-ins also use `authenticated`, unlike requests without a session. Service-role credentials bypass RLS and must remain server-side. [RLS documentation](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security)

## 2. Authentication methods and configuration

Supabase Auth establishes identity; RLS provides authorization. Supported methods include:

- Email/password and passwordless email magic links or OTPs.
- Phone/SMS authentication.
- Social OAuth providers, including Google, GitHub, Apple and Microsoft.
- Enterprise SAML SSO, custom OAuth/OIDC providers, and anonymous sign-in.
- MFA through authenticator-app TOTP or phone verification.  
[Auth overview](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth) · [MFA documentation](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/auth-mfa)

Social providers are enabled in the Dashboard; phone authentication uses a configured messaging provider such as Twilio, MessageBird or Vonage. Auth issues JWTs that supply identity to database and Storage policies. MFA-sensitive policies can require the JWT’s `aal` claim to equal `aal2`. [Auth overview](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth) · [MFA documentation](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/auth-mfa)

**Evidence limitation:** The captured sources do not establish provider-specific client-ID/secret fields, callback URLs or SAML setup steps; consult the relevant provider guide for those details.

## 3. Storage access policies

Storage uses the same PostgreSQL RLS engine, applied to **`storage.objects`**. Its policies are separate from application-table policies: protecting a database record does not automatically protect its associated file. [Architecture guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/getting-started/the-supabase-way-to-build)

Policies can restrict access by bucket, user identity, ownership or folder path. Uploads require INSERT permission; overwriting through upsert additionally requires SELECT and UPDATE permissions. [Storage access control](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage/security/access-control)

- **Private buckets:** Downloads and other operations require authorization; files can be accessed with an authorized JWT or temporary signed URL.
- **Public buckets:** Anyone with the file URL can retrieve it, but uploads, deletions, moves and copies remain access-controlled.  
[Bucket fundamentals](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage/buckets/fundamentals)

Service keys bypass Storage RLS too—never expose them in browser or mobile clients. [Storage access control](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage/security/access-control)

## Dependency injection

Declare a dependency by passing its callable—not calling it—to `Depends()`. FastAPI resolves its parameters, runs it, and injects its return value into the endpoint. The recommended declaration uses `Annotated`:

```python
async def pagination(skip: int = 0, limit: int = 100):
    return {"skip": skip, "limit": limit}

@app.get("/items/")
async def items(params: Annotated[dict, Depends(pagination)]):
    return params
```

Dependencies can themselves have dependencies, and their request parameters appear in the generated OpenAPI documentation. Both synchronous and asynchronous dependencies are supported, regardless of the endpoint’s style. [Dependencies documentation](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/dependencies/)

By default, a dependency shared across a request’s dependency tree runs once; FastAPI reuses its result **within that request**. Use `Depends(dependency, use_cache=False)` to request fresh execution. This is not cross-request caching. [Sub-dependencies](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/dependencies/sub-dependencies/)

## Request validation

FastAPI uses type annotations to parse, convert, and validate incoming data:

- Parameters matching URL placeholders are path parameters.
- Ordinary scalar parameters generally become query parameters.
- Pydantic model parameters become request bodies.

For example, `item_id: int` requests integer parsing, while `item: Item` validates JSON against the Pydantic `Item` model. A default such as `= None` makes a parameter optional; merely allowing `None` in its type does not make omission optional. [Request bodies](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body/)

Declarations such as `Query()`, `Path()`, and `Body()` add constraints, including numeric bounds, string lengths, and patterns. [Parameter reference](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/reference/parameters/)

Reading data directly from `Request` bypasses automatic validation, conversion, and documentation for that data. [Using Request directly](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/using-request-directly/)

**Evidence gap:** The captured official pages establish automatic validation but do not establish the default validation-error status and payload or custom exception-handler behavior. The research returned those details only from an outside-domain source, which is excluded here.

## Async handling

The documentation’s practical rules are:

- Use **`async def`** when calling libraries whose operations must be awaited.
- Use **plain `def`** for blocking I/O libraries without awaitable APIs.
- Prefer `async def` when no waiting is involved; if uncertain, the documentation suggests `def`.
- You may mix both endpoint styles. Python permits `await` only inside `async def`.

FastAPI runs synchronous endpoints in a thread pool; putting blocking I/O directly inside an asynchronous endpoint can instead block the event loop. Async chiefly helps overlap waiting—it does not automatically parallelize CPU-intensive work. [Concurrency and async/await](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/async/)

## Tokenizer construction, training and loading

A tokenizer is a configurable text-processing pipeline: **normalization → pre-tokenization → tokenization model → post-processing**, with a decoder for converting tokens back to text. The tokenization model, such as BPE, determines how text becomes vocabulary IDs; other components control splitting, normalization and special-token handling. [Tokenizer API](https://huggingface.co/docs/tokenizers/v0.23.3/api/tokenizer)

In Transformers, a practical training route is to start from a model-specific tokenizer and call:

```python
new_tokenizer = tokenizer.train_new_from_iterator(
    corpus, vocab_size=1000
)
```

This retains the starting tokenizer’s processing configuration while learning a new vocabulary. `AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("organization/model")` loads a compatible tokenizer from the Hub; `save_pretrained("./tokenizer")` saves its artifacts for later loading. At the lower level, `Tokenizer.from_file("tokenizer.json")` loads a serialized tokenizer. [Transformers tokenizer guide](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/fast_tokenizers), [Tokenizer API](https://huggingface.co/docs/tokenizers/v0.23.3/api/tokenizer)

**Evidence limitation:** the returned extraction incompletely covered low-level training and saving methods. Its assertion that the bare `Tokenizer` has no training methods is not sufficiently supported and is not relied upon here.

## Pipeline task abstraction

Transformers’ `pipeline()` combines a model with its appropriate tokenizer or processor and exposes **preprocessing → inference → post-processing** through one task-oriented callable. It can select default components or accept a specified model. This simplifies inference across text, images, audio and multimodal tasks. [Pipeline guide](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/pipeline_tutorial)

```python
from transformers import pipeline

generate = pipeline("text-generation", model="google/gemma-2-2b")
result = generate("The secret to baking is")
```

Inputs and outputs remain task-specific: text generation accepts text and returns generated-text records; speech recognition accepts audio and returns transcribed text; image classification returns labels and scores. Lists, datasets and generators support processing multiple inputs, but batching is not necessarily faster. [Pipeline guide](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/pipeline_tutorial)

## Model repository versioning and pinning

Hub repositories are Git-versioned. Loading APIs accept a `revision` identifying a **branch, tag or commit**; model loading defaults to `"main"`. Pull-request revisions can also be referenced as `refs/pr/<number>`. [Model API](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/v5.21.0/main_classes/model)

```python
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(
    "organization/model",
    revision="<commit-hash>"
)
```

For reproducible runs, prefer an explicit commit hash over a moving branch. Tokenizer loading and `pipeline()` also expose revision selection; when assembling components separately, pin them consistently to the intended repository versions. [Model sharing](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/v5.22.1/model_sharing), [Tokenizer API](https://huggingface.co/docs/tokenizers/v0.23.3/api/tokenizer), [Pipeline API](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/main_classes/pipelines)

The captured documentation spans multiple releases, so exact signatures and output details should be checked against the installed library version.

## Spawning versus cancellation

- **`tokio::spawn` creates an independently scheduled task**, returning a `JoinHandle` for observing completion. Execution starts without awaiting the handle, but `spawn` never synchronously polls the future. Tasks may move between worker threads; both the future and its output require `Send + 'static`. Runtime shutdown can drop outstanding tasks before completion. ([spawn reference](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/task/fn.spawn.html))
- **`'static` does not mean “runs forever.”** It means the spawned future cannot depend on borrowed data with a shorter lifetime. `async move` commonly transfers ownership into the task. Values retained across `.await` must satisfy the task’s `Send` requirement. ([Tokio spawning tutorial](https://tokio.rs/tokio/tutorial/spawning))
- **Cancellation is cooperative, not preemptive.** Aborting schedules cancellation; the task must yield before cancellation can take effect. Cancellation drops the future and runs destructors for its live local values. Consequently, code that keeps running without yielding cannot be promptly interrupted. ([Task documentation](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/task/))
- **`abort()` requests cancellation; it does not wait for cleanup.** Await the `JoinHandle` to observe termination. A cancelled task produces a `JoinError`, but normal completion can win a race with an abort request. Repeated abort calls are harmless. A running `spawn_blocking` task cannot be aborted. ([Task documentation](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/task/))

## Timeouts and `select!`: evidence limits

The returned evidence only briefly describes these mechanisms:

| Mechanism | Supported comparison |
|---|---|
| `timeout(duration, future)` | Bounds waiting for a future and returns `Err(Elapsed)` when it does not complete in time. |
| `select!` | Waits on multiple branches concurrently, completing when the first finishes. |

These descriptions appear in the captured synthesis attributed to the [task documentation](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/task/), **not dedicated timeout or `select!` documentation**, so they provide weaker coverage.

**Not established by the captured pages:** timeout polling/deadline subtleties; whether timing out a spawned task stops that task; `select!` losing-branch cancellation, cancellation safety, fairness, `biased;`, or disabled-branch behavior. Those distinctions are essential for a complete comparison and should not be inferred from the spawn/abort evidence.

**Source-scope limitation:** although the prescribed search requested `tokio.rs`, three of the four returned pages were on `docs.rs`. The four-page allowance was exhausted; no additional pages were fetched.

## Schema migration: schema → database

1. **Edit `schema.prisma`**, then run:
   ```bash
   npx prisma migrate dev --name describe_change
   ```
   Prisma replays migration history in a **shadow database** to detect drift, applies pending migrations there, generates a migration from schema changes, then applies unapplied migrations to the development database. It also updates **`_prisma_migrations`**, the database’s applied-migration records. [Development command documentation](https://docs.prisma.io/docs/cli/v7/migrate/dev)

2. **To generate a migration without applying it:**
   ```bash
   npx prisma migrate dev --create-only
   ```
   This creates the migration file without applying the new migration to the development database. [Documentation](https://docs.prisma.io/docs/cli/v7/migrate/dev)

3. **Regenerate Prisma Client explicitly:**
   ```bash
   npx prisma generate
   ```
   This generates client artifacts. The v7 documentation explicitly says `migrate dev` no longer automatically runs generation or seed scripts. [Documentation](https://docs.prisma.io/docs/cli/v7/migrate/dev)

4. **Apply existing migrations in staging/production:**
   ```bash
   npx prisma migrate deploy
   ```
   This applies pending migrations and records them in `_prisma_migrations`; it does **not** generate new migrations. [Migration command reference](https://www.prisma.io/docs/cli/v7/migrate)

### Other migration commands and their effects

| Command | What changes |
|---|---|
| `prisma migrate status` | Nothing; compares migration files with `_prisma_migrations` records and reports status. |
| `prisma migrate resolve` | Changes applied-state records for baselining or migration recovery; does not execute the migration’s DDL. |
| `prisma migrate diff` | Outputs differences between schema sources, optionally as SQL; does not itself apply them. |
| `prisma migrate reset` | **Destructively removes data/tables**, then reapplies migrations; development only. |

Source: [Migration command reference](https://www.prisma.io/docs/cli/v7/migrate).

## Database introspection: database → schema

1. Configure the database connection through `prisma.config.ts`.
2. Run:
   ```bash
   npx prisma db pull
   ```
   This reverse-engineers the existing database into **`prisma/schema.prisma`**—the documented output is the Prisma schema, rather than a migration.
3. Run:
   ```bash
   npx prisma generate
   ```
   This regenerates Prisma Client from that schema. [CLI reference](https://docs.prisma.io/docs/orm/reference/prisma-cli-reference)

**Evidence limits:** The captured pages cover introspection only briefly; they do not establish detailed `db pull` options, overwrite/merge behavior, or output-format controls. The generation behavior above follows the explicit v7 note, despite conflicting generic wording in the returned summary.

## When to choose each

- **MergeTree family:** The general-purpose choice for high ingestion rates and large datasets, especially when you need sorting, sparse primary-key indexes, partitioning, replication, or specialized merge-time processing. However, ClickHouse describes these engines as relatively heavyweight and advises against creating many small MergeTree tables. [MergeTree reference](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/engines/table-engines/mergetree-family/mergetree), [family overview](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/engines/table-engines/mergetree-family/)
- **Log family:** Explicitly recommended when you need **many small tables**, such as tables holding temporary data. The captured evidence does not establish more detailed selection criteria. [Family overview](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/engines/table-engines/mergetree-family/)

## Compression and insertion behaviour

**MergeTree** writes inserts into immutable, sorted, compressed **data parts**. The captured quickstart identifies LZ4 as the default compression. Sorting helps compression by placing similar values together; consequently, sorting-key design affects both query performance and storage efficiency. [Quickstart](https://clickhouse.com/docs/get-started/quickstarts/create-your-first-mergetree-table), [reference](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/engines/table-engines/mergetree-family/mergetree)

Parts can use **Wide** storage—separate files per column—or **Compact** storage—a single file for all columns. The reference recommends Compact parts for small, frequent inserts. These are physical layouts, not different compression algorithms. [Reference](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/engines/table-engines/mergetree-family/mergetree)

**Log family:** Its compression defaults, file layouts, and insertion mechanics were not documented in the captured pages, so a reliable side-by-side comparison is unavailable.

## Merge semantics

For **MergeTree**, background processing combines smaller parts into larger parts. **Parts in different partitions are never merged.** Ordinary MergeTree merging should not be confused with row deduplication: specialized family members provide additional semantics. [Quickstart](https://clickhouse.com/docs/get-started/quickstarts/create-your-first-mergetree-table), [reference](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/engines/table-engines/mergetree-family/mergetree)

Examples include `ReplacingMergeTree` for duplicate replacement, `SummingMergeTree` for summation, and `AggregatingMergeTree` for combining aggregate states. Background processing means those transformations need not be complete immediately after insertion. [Family overview](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/engines/table-engines/mergetree-family/), [AggregatingMergeTree](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/engines/table-engines/mergetree-family/aggregatingmergetree)

**Evidence limitation:** All four retrieved pages covered MergeTree; only the family overview mentioned Log. Thus, the supported conclusion is **MergeTree for substantial analytical workloads; consider Log for many small temporary tables**. Whether and how Log engines compress or merge data remains unverified in this evidence set.

### How data fetching works

React Server Components execute **on the server, not in the browser**—either at build time or per request. They can be asynchronous: a component can `await` a database query, filesystem read, or network request directly while rendering, then return UI based on the result. Server-only code and dependencies stay out of the browser bundle. [React documentation](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/server-components)

### What the client receives

The client receives the **rendered result**, not executable Server Component code. Server Components can compose Client Components, whose JavaScript runs in the browser to provide interactivity. Server Components themselves cannot use client-side state APIs such as `useState`. [React documentation](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/server-components)

The server-to-client boundary is a serialization boundary: values crossing it must be representable by React’s supported serialization mechanism. This is not the same as shipping the server component or its database-access code to the browser.

### Streaming and Suspense

Not every data request must finish before the server can begin returning UI. A Server Component can start an asynchronous operation and pass its pending promise to a Client Component. The Client Component reads it with `use()`, while a surrounding `<Suspense>` boundary displays a fallback until the result is ready. This allows server-started data fetching to integrate with progressively delivered UI. [React documentation](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/server-components)

**Evidence limitation:** The research tool returned one react.dev page and three Next.js pages despite the requested domain restriction. The explanation above relies on the React source; framework-specific details—such as exactly how initial HTML, serialized payloads, and navigation responses are packaged—are not established here from react.dev evidence.

**Streaming changes when results arrive; Suspense defines what users see while waiting.**

- **Start work on the server:** A Server Component can begin fetching data without awaiting it immediately, then pass the pending promise to a Client Component that reads it with `use()`. The browser does not need to restart that fetch after mounting. [React](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/server-components)
- **Show a fallback while waiting:** If that read suspends, the nearest `<Suspense>` boundary displays its fallback—for example, “Loading posts…”—until the promise resolves. This allows loading UI to appear before the requested data is ready, rather than requiring every request to finish first. [React](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/server-components)
- **Deliver the result later:** Once the promise resolves, React can display the resolved content instead of the fallback. What crosses the boundary is the server-produced result/data, **not the Server Component’s executable source code**. Streaming does not move server execution into the browser. [React](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/server-components)

For example, a page can start `getPosts()`, immediately return a Suspense-wrapped posts component, show its loading fallback while the request is pending, and reveal the posts when ready. [React](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/server-components)

**Evidence limits:** The saved report supports this conceptual sequence, but does not establish exact network chunk formats, flush timing, or delivery order. It also contains Next.js-specific explanations despite the original react.dev restriction; those are not treated here as React-wide guarantees.

## Standard error model

gRPC reports success or failure using a **status code** and an optional human-readable error message. `OK` (`0`) means success. This model works across supported languages and is independent of protobuf, but does not itself carry structured error details. [Error handling](https://grpc.io/docs/guides/error/)

## Status codes

The standard codes are:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `0 OK` | Success |
| `1 CANCELLED` | Operation cancelled |
| `2 UNKNOWN` | Unknown or insufficiently described error |
| `3 INVALID_ARGUMENT` | Invalid argument regardless of system state |
| `4 DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` | Deadline expired |
| `5 NOT_FOUND` | Requested entity absent |
| `6 ALREADY_EXISTS` | Entity already exists |
| `7 PERMISSION_DENIED` | Caller lacks permission |
| `8 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` | Quota or resource exhausted |
| `9 FAILED_PRECONDITION` | System state prevents execution |
| `10 ABORTED` | Operation aborted, often because of concurrency |
| `11 OUT_OF_RANGE` | Operation exceeds the valid range |
| `12 UNIMPLEMENTED` | Operation unsupported |
| `13 INTERNAL` | Internal error or broken invariant |
| `14 UNAVAILABLE` | Service currently unavailable |
| `15 DATA_LOSS` | Unrecoverable data loss or corruption |
| `16 UNAUTHENTICATED` | Missing or invalid authentication |

Both application code and gRPC libraries can produce errors. Notably, `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` does **not** prove that a state-changing operation failed—it may have completed before its response arrived. [Status-code reference](https://grpc.github.io/grpc/core/md_doc_statuscodes.html)

## Retry semantics and service configuration

The important distinction is:

- **`UNAVAILABLE`:** retry the individual call when safe.
- **`ABORTED`:** retry a higher-level operation, such as an entire transaction.
- **`FAILED_PRECONDITION`:** fix the system state before retrying.

There is no universally retryable set of codes. Applications must decide which failures warrant retry; retrying non-idempotent operations can be unsafe. [Status-code reference](https://grpc.github.io/grpc/core/md_doc_statuscodes.html)

**Evidence gap:** the retrieved pages did not cover service-configuration syntax or configured retry-policy behavior. Consequently, they do not establish attempt limits, backoff settings, or how retryable codes are configured.

## Rich error details

For protobuf-based services, gRPC supports Google's richer error model: additional typed protobuf messages describe problems such as invalid parameters, quota violations, or debugging information. These details travel in trailing response metadata. [Error handling](https://grpc.io/docs/guides/error/)

Support and payload expectations vary by language. Rich details also have operational costs: ordinary HTTP proxies and loggers may not expose them, they can reduce HTTP/2 header-compression efficiency, and oversized details can exceed header limits—potentially obscuring the original error. [Error handling](https://grpc.io/docs/guides/error/)

**Source limitation:** although the requested domain was `grpc.io`, the controlled research tool also returned official gRPC references hosted on `grpc.github.io`; those supply the complete code table and retry distinctions above.

## What at-least-once delivery means

**A message can be delivered more than once.** Acknowledgements let RabbitMQ and clients determine when responsibility has transferred and when retransmission may be needed after a failure. Consumers should therefore be **idempotent**: processing the same message again should not repeat its business effects. [RabbitMQ reliability guide](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/reliability)

## How consumers acknowledge messages

RabbitMQ supports two acknowledgement modes:

- **Automatic acknowledgement (`autoAck=true`):** RabbitMQ considers the message delivered when it is written to the connection socket—not when processing finishes. If the consumer fails before processing it, the message can be lost.
- **Manual acknowledgement (`autoAck=false`):** The consumer explicitly reports the delivery’s outcome. This is the appropriate mode for at-least-once processing. [Acknowledgements guide](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms)

With manual acknowledgements, **acknowledge only after completing the required work**, such as recording the result in a database. Once acknowledged, RabbitMQ can delete the message. [Reliability guide](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/reliability)

The AMQP methods are:

| Method | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `basic.ack` | Processing succeeded; RabbitMQ can discard the message. |
| `basic.reject` | Reject one delivery; request requeueing or discard/dead-letter it. |
| `basic.nack` | Negative acknowledgement that also supports multiple deliveries. |

Each delivery has a **channel-scoped delivery tag**. Acknowledge it on the **same channel** that received it. With `multiple=true`, an acknowledgement covers all outstanding deliveries up to and including that tag. [Acknowledgements guide](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms)

For example, after successful processing in the Java client:

```java
channel.basicAck(deliveryTag, false);
```

To request another attempt:

```java
channel.basicReject(deliveryTag, true);
```

Repeated requeueing can create expensive redelivery loops, so retries need limits or another failure-handling strategy. [Acknowledgements guide](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms)

## Publisher confirms are separate

**Consumer acknowledgements flow from consumer to broker; publisher confirms flow from broker to publisher.** They are independent: a publisher confirm does not establish that a consumer completed processing. Pairing publisher confirms with manual consumer acknowledgements addresses both sides of delivery. Lost confirms can lead publishers to retransmit, another reason duplicates must be safe. [Acknowledgements guide](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms), [Reliability guide](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/reliability)

**Transactions coverage gap:** The retrieved evidence did not cover AMQP transaction semantics (`tx.select`/`tx.commit`), so it does not support a detailed comparison of transactions and publisher confirms.

**The saved report is insufficient for a full comparison with transacted publishing:** it explicitly says AMQP transactions (`tx.select`/`tx.commit`) were not covered.

What it does establish:

- **Publisher confirms are broker-to-publisher acknowledgements.** They indicate that the broker received and acted upon a publication, transferring responsibility to the broker—not merely that TCP delivered bytes. [Reliability guide](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/reliability)
- **They do not guarantee consumer processing.** Consumer acknowledgements are separate and independent; a publisher confirm is not evidence that a consumer completed its business operation. [Acknowledgements and confirms guide](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms)
- **They do not provide exactly-once delivery.** A confirm can be lost, prompting retransmission and duplicate messages. Consumers therefore need idempotent processing. [Reliability guide](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/reliability)

**Unresolved from this evidence:** how transaction commits differ from confirms, transaction atomicity and rollback guarantees, performance differences, and the precise persistence or replication conditions required before confirmation. Answering those points would require evidence not captured in the saved report.

## Workspace manifest structure

pnpm uses **`pnpm-workspace.yaml` at the repository root** to define a workspace. The root package is always included. The manifest contains package-selection patterns, dependency catalogs, and configuration settings. ([Workspace documentation](https://pnpm.io/workspaces), [official documentation source](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm.io/blob/main/docs/settings.md))

For example:

```yaml
packages:
  - 'packages/*'
  - 'components/**'
  - '!**/test/**'

catalog:
  chalk: ^4.1.2

catalogs:
  react16:
    react: ^16.7.0
    react-dom: ^16.7.0
```

- **`packages`** selects directories using include and exclude globs.
- **`catalog`** defines the default dependency-version catalog.
- **`catalogs`** defines named catalogs.
- Other configuration keys appear at the top level. **`packageConfigs`** supports per-project settings, either as a project-keyed map or as an array of entries with `match` patterns. Per-project settings require separate lockfiles (`sharedWorkspaceLockfile: false`); with the default shared lockfile, ignored entries are reported. ([Documentation source](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm.io/blob/main/docs/settings.md))

## Configuring hoisting

The captured documentation identifies hoisting controls as **workspace-file-only settings**, because they determine the `node_modules` structure. Its listed controls include: ([Documentation source](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm.io/blob/main/docs/settings.md))

| Setting | Documented purpose |
|---|---|
| `hoist` | Controls dependency hoisting. |
| `hoistPattern` | Selects packages for hoisting using glob patterns. |
| `publicHoistPattern` | Hoists matching packages into top-level `node_modules`, making them visible to application code. |
| `hoistWorkspacePackages` | Controls hoisting of workspace packages. |
| `shamefullyHoist` | Compatibility option for a flat, npm/Yarn-style layout. |
| `hoistingLimits` | Controls hoisting boundaries. |

An illustrative configuration is:

```yaml
packages:
  - 'packages/*'

nodeLinker: isolated
hoistPattern:
  - '*eslint*'
publicHoistPattern:
  - '*types*'
shamefullyHoist: false
```

**Hoisting is distinct from workspace linking.** `linkWorkspacePackages` controls whether compatible local workspace packages are linked; the `workspace:` dependency protocol explicitly requires local resolution rather than registry fallback. ([Workspace documentation](https://pnpm.io/workspaces))

**Evidence limitations:** The returned evidence did not establish detailed defaults or full semantics for every hoisting setting. Although the search was restricted to `pnpm.io`, it also returned the official documentation’s GitHub source files; those are cited explicitly above rather than represented as fetched pnpm.io pages.

## Null and absence are different

JSONata treats **`null` as an actual value**, whereas an absent value is represented by an **empty sequence**, meaning “nothing” or “no match.” `null` is a supported data type; absence is not. [Processing model](https://docs.jsonata.org/processing)

### Path expressions
- A path matching a field whose value is `null` returns **`null`**.
- A path that does not exist returns **nothing**, described in the documentation as JavaScript `undefined`; missing input data does **not** cause an error.
- An out-of-range array index likewise returns nothing. [Simple queries](https://docs.jsonata.org/simple)

The documented examples illustrate the distinction:

```text
Other.Misc     → null       (field exists)
Other.Nothing  → nothing    (field does not exist)
Phone[8]       → nothing    (index out of range)
```

### Output and sequence rules
An empty sequence does not appear in expression output. If an object-construction expression assigns an empty sequence to a property, **that property is omitted**, rather than emitted with a `null` value.

A singleton sequence is equivalent to its sole value, so a single matched `null` remains `null`. Nested result sequences are flattened; missing results are not converted into null placeholders. [Processing model](https://docs.jsonata.org/processing)

### Predicates
The processing model describes a filter, `seq[expr]`, as applying the bracketed predicate to each item and retaining matching items. A filter with no matches produces the no-match/empty-sequence outcome—not a `null` placeholder. [Processing model](https://docs.jsonata.org/processing)

**Evidence limitation:** The retrieved documentation does not establish the Boolean conversion of `null` or absence inside predicates, or their exact behavior with equality operators. Those details cannot be concluded from this evidence alone.

## 1. Ingress routing

An **Ingress** defines external HTTP/HTTPS routing to cluster Services. An **Ingress controller** must implement it; creating the resource alone does not route traffic. `spec.ingressClassName` selects the IngressClass responsible for handling it. [Kubernetes Ingress documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/ingress/)

Example:

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: shop
spec:
  ingressClassName: example-controller
  rules:
  - host: shop.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /catalog
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: catalog
            port:
              number: 80
```

Here, requests matching `shop.example.com` and `/catalog` route to Service `catalog`, port `80`.

Path matching supports:
- **Exact:** case-sensitive, complete-path match.
- **Prefix:** slash-delimited prefix; `/catalog/items` matches `/catalog`, but `/catalogue` does not.
- **ImplementationSpecific:** controller-defined behavior.

The longest matching path wins; an `Exact` match wins a tie with `Prefix`. `spec.defaultBackend` can handle unmatched requests. [Ingress documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/ingress/)

## 2. TLS termination

TLS termination means the ingress layer handles the client's encrypted connection using a certificate and private key. Kubernetes documents configuring these through a Secret containing `tls.crt` and `tls.key`, referenced by `spec.tls[].secretName`. [Kubernetes TLS example](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2016/03/kubernetes-1-2-and-simplifying-advanced-networking-with-ingress/)

The relevant configuration fragment is:

```yaml
spec:
  tls:
  - secretName: shop-tls
```

**Evidence limitation:** the captured TLS example uses the obsolete `extensions/v1beta1` API. The current documentation was truncated before its TLS section, so these results do not verify the complete modern host-to-certificate configuration. Do not copy the historical Ingress manifest wholesale. Its demonstrated HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect should also not be assumed universal across controllers.

## 3. Path rewriting

**Matching a path and rewriting it are different operations.** Core Ingress path rules select backends; rewriting is controller-specific, commonly configured through annotations. [Ingress documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/ingress/)

For ingress-nginx:

```yaml
metadata:
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: "/uuid"
```

With a matching `/IP` rule, the backend receives `/uuid` instead of `/IP`. This is an internal rewrite, not a client redirect. Importantly, Kubernetes’ ingress-nginx migration guidance reports that `rewrite-target` enables regex matching across the entire host, potentially changing other paths’ matching behavior. Do not assume these annotations or semantics work with another controller. [Kubernetes rewrite example and caveats](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/02/27/ingress-nginx-before-you-migrate/)

## Static analysis and rules

Stylelint checks stylesheet source against configured rules to **catch errors and enforce conventions**, without executing it. Its rule index groups checks into “Avoid errors” (such as invalid syntax, duplicates and unknown identifiers) and “Enforce conventions” (such as allowed/disallowed features and complexity limits). [Rules](https://stylelint.io/user-guide/rules/)

Configure rules under `rules`, usually extending a shared configuration such as `stylelint-config-standard`. Local settings customize inherited rules; plugins provide additional, namespaced rules. Rule primary options have rule-specific meanings—for example, `selector-max-id: 0` prohibits ID selectors; **zero is not a general disable switch**. [Customizing](https://stylelint.io/user-guide/customize/)

Rules can use `[primaryOption, secondaryOptions]`. Severity defaults to `"error"`; set `severity: "warning"` to report a warning instead. Use `null` to disable a rule. Lowering severity does not ignore the code. [Configuring](https://stylelint.io/user-guide/configure/)

```json
{
  "extends": ["stylelint-config-standard"],
  "rules": {
    "color-no-invalid-hex": [true, { "severity": "warning" }],
    "selector-max-id": 0,
    "block-no-empty": null
  }
}
```

## Automatic fixing

Run:

```sh
stylelint "**/*.css" --fix
```

Only rules marked 🔧 in the rule index support automatic fixing. Examples include certain deprecated-syntax replacements, spacing around `calc()` operators, removing vendor prefixes and removing units from zero lengths. Other violations still require manual changes. [Rules](https://stylelint.io/user-guide/rules/)

The `fix` option supports:
- **`"strict"`**, the default: fixes only when there are no syntax errors.
- **`"lax"`**: uses a safe parser to fix as much as possible despite syntax errors.

Set a rule’s secondary option `disableFix: true` to retain its checking without applying fixes. Legacy rules using deprecated `context.fix` have broader disable-comment restrictions: a relevant disable comment can prevent fixing throughout the source. [Options](https://stylelint.io/user-guide/options/)

## Ignoring files and code

**Whole files:** use `.stylelintignore`, with `.gitignore`-style patterns relative to the working directory, or configuration’s `ignoreFiles`. CLI options include `--ignore-path` and `--ignore-pattern`. `node_modules` is ignored by default unless `--disable-default-ignores` is supplied. [Ignoring code](https://stylelint.io/user-guide/ignore-code/) · [CLI](https://stylelint.io/user-guide/cli/)

**Specific regions or lines:**

```css
/* stylelint-disable declaration-no-important */
a { color: red !important; }
/* stylelint-enable declaration-no-important */

/* stylelint-disable-next-line color-no-invalid-hex */
a { color: #xyz; }
```

`stylelint-disable-line` suppresses the current line. Omitting rule names disables all rules in scope. Disabled code also bypasses applicable autofixes. Reasons can follow ` -- `. [Ignoring code](https://stylelint.io/user-guide/ignore-code/)

Audit exceptions with `reportNeedlessDisables`, `reportDescriptionlessDisables`, `reportInvalidScopeDisables` and `reportUnscopedDisables`; `--ignore-disables` exposes violations hidden by comments. [Options](https://stylelint.io/user-guide/options/)

**Evidence limitation:** captured material did not establish detailed `ignoreFiles` or suppression-file semantics.

## Controlling overlap

The captured GitHub Enterprise Server 3.11 documentation supports two scopes:

- **Workflow-level `concurrency`:** limits entire workflow runs.
- **`jobs.<job_id>.concurrency`:** limits a particular job.

A concurrency group permits **at most one running and one pending** job or workflow run. A newly queued member replaces an existing pending member; `cancel-in-progress: true` also cancels a running member. Thus, retaining the running job does **not** imply a durable queue of every invocation.
```yaml
on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true
```

Including `github.workflow` helps avoid unintended cancellation between different workflows sharing a group. [Concurrency controls](https://docs.github.com/en/enterprise-server@3.11/actions/writing-workflows/choosing-what-your-workflow-does/control-the-concurrency-of-workflows-and-jobs)

HTTP caching separates **whether a response may be stored** from **how long it may be reused without checking the origin**.

### Storage controls

- **`no-store`**: private and shared HTTP caches must not store the response.
- **`private`**: permits storage in a private cache, such as a browser, but not a shared cache.
- **`public`**: explicitly permits shared-cache storage, including certain responses that would otherwise be restricted.
- **`no-cache`**: permits storage, but requires successful validation before each reuse. **It does not mean `no-store`.**  
[MDN: Cache-Control](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control)

### Freshness lifetime

- **`max-age=N`**: sets the freshness lifetime in seconds. A response’s existing age counts toward that lifetime; downloading it from a shared cache does not restart the clock.
- **`s-maxage=N`**: sets freshness for shared caches only, overriding `max-age` and `Expires` there.
- **`Expires`**: supplies an absolute expiration date. `max-age` takes precedence when both are present.
- Without explicit freshness information, caches may calculate a heuristic lifetime; that behavior is implementation-dependent.  
[MDN: Cache-Control](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control) · [MDN: HTTP caching](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Caching)

For example, `max-age=3600` with `Age: 600` leaves approximately **3,000 seconds of freshness**. [MDN: HTTP caching](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Caching)

### Revalidation and stale responses

- **`must-revalidate`**: allows reuse while fresh, but requires validation once stale; the cache cannot simply serve stale content if validation is unavailable.
- **`proxy-revalidate`**: applies the same restriction only to shared caches.
- **`immutable`**: indicates that the response will not change while fresh—useful for versioned or content-hashed asset URLs.
- **`stale-while-revalidate`**: permits temporary stale reuse while refreshing in the background.
- **`stale-if-error`**: permits stale reuse when an origin error occurs, within the specified allowance.  
[MDN: Cache-Control](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control)

Validation uses response validators:

| Response header | Conditional request header |
|---|---|
| `ETag` | `If-None-Match` |
| `Last-Modified` | `If-Modified-Since` |

If unchanged, the server can return **`304 Not Modified`**, allowing reuse of the stored body without retransmitting it. [MDN: HTTP caching](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Caching)

**Scope caveat:** These are HTTP-cache rules, not a complete description of programmatic Service Worker caching. Browser history restoration also does not necessarily trigger revalidation. [MDN: PWA caching](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Progressive_web_apps/Guides/Caching) · [MDN: Cache-Control](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control)

When a response becomes **stale**, the main difference is whether the cache must wait for validation or may serve the old response immediately.

| Directive | Behavior after becoming stale |
|---|---|
| **`must-revalidate`** | Must validate with the origin before reuse. If validation is unavailable, return `504 Gateway Timeout` rather than serve stale content. |
| **`proxy-revalidate`** | Same requirement, but only for shared caches. |
| **`no-cache`** | Also requires validation before reuse—but unlike `must-revalidate`, it requires validation **even while fresh**. Storage is still allowed. |
| **`stale-while-revalidate`** | Allows stale content to be served while an update happens in the background, avoiding a wait for that update. |
| **`stale-if-error`** | Allows stale content as a fallback when the origin encounters an error, rather than as the normal background-refresh strategy. |

These distinctions are documented in [MDN’s Cache-Control reference](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control).

### How validation checks for changes

Two documented mechanisms use conditional requests:

- **Modification time:** the cached response’s `Last-Modified` value is sent as `If-Modified-Since`.
- **Entity identifier:** the cached response’s `ETag` is sent as `If-None-Match`.

If unchanged, the origin returns **`304 Not Modified`** without retransmitting the body; the cache can refresh and reuse its stored response. Staleness therefore does **not** automatically mean discarding or downloading the entire response. [MDN: HTTP caching](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Caching)

### Service Worker strategies are separate

The saved report also documents a programmatic **Network First** strategy: try the network, cache a successful response, and fall back to a cached response if the network request fails. This is application-controlled behavior, not itself an HTTP revalidation directive. [MDN: PWA caching](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Progressive_web_apps/Guides/Caching)

**Evidence limits:** The saved report supports these high-level distinctions, but does not capture detailed stale-window limits, qualifying error conditions, or a full comparison of all Service Worker strategies. It also notes that browser history restoration may bypass ordinary revalidation expectations. [MDN: Cache-Control](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control)

## What linked worktrees are

A **linked worktree** is an additional working directory attached to an existing Git repository. It lets you work on another branch without disturbing changes in your current directory—or making a separate clone.

Worktrees share the repository’s object database and most refs, but each has its own `HEAD`, index (staging area), and working files. Git also maintains administrative metadata for each linked worktree. [Git documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree/2.54.0.html)

## Creating one

Run these commands from an existing repository:

```bash
# Check out an existing branch in another directory
git worktree add ../project-hotfix hotfix

# Create a new branch based on HEAD
git worktree add -b emergency-fix ../project-fix

# Create a detached-HEAD worktree for temporary investigation
git worktree add --detach ../project-test HEAD
```

`git worktree add <path> [<commit-ish>]` creates the directory and checks out the requested branch or commit. Without a commit or branch argument, Git normally uses the directory’s basename as the branch name, creating that branch from `HEAD` if necessary. By default, Git refuses to check out a branch already checked out in another worktree. [Git documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree/2.54.0.html)

## Listing and removing worktrees

```bash
git worktree list
git worktree list --porcelain   # Stable format for scripts
git worktree remove ../project-fix
```

Listing shows the main worktree first, followed by linked worktrees. Removal normally requires a clean worktree; `--force` permits removal of an unclean one, so use it carefully. The main worktree cannot be removed with this command. [Git documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree/2.54.0.html)

## Data retention and cleanup

- **Shared repository data:** Worktrees share objects and most refs; their working files and staging state are separate.
- **Stale metadata:** If you manually delete a worktree directory, its administrative files can remain. `git worktree prune` removes stale administrative files; automatic cleanup is controlled by `gc.worktreePruneExpire`.
- **Temporarily unavailable directories:** For a worktree on a removable or intermittently mounted drive, use `git worktree lock <path>` to prevent its metadata from being pruned. A lock also protects against normal movement or removal. [Git documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree/2.54.0.html)

**Retention caveat:** The captured evidence establishes metadata cleanup behavior, not a guarantee that uncommitted work remains recoverable after forced removal. Commit or otherwise preserve needed changes before deleting a worktree.

- **List worktrees:** `git worktree list` shows the main worktree followed by linked worktrees. For scripts, use `git worktree list --porcelain -z` for stable, NUL-terminated output. [Git documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree/2.54.0.html)

- **Remove a linked worktree:** `git worktree remove <path>`. By default, Git only removes clean worktrees. `git worktree remove --force <path>` permits removal of an unclean worktree; removing a locked worktree requires `--force` twice. The main worktree cannot be removed this way. [Git documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree/2.54.0.html)

**What happens to uncommitted files?** Normal removal refuses an unclean worktree, protecting pending work. Forced removal bypasses that protection: treat uncommitted files as at risk and commit, stash, or back them up first. **The saved report does not explicitly establish the precise deletion or recoverability behavior for each category of uncommitted file**, so it is insufficient to promise recovery after forced removal.

`git worktree prune` is different: it cleans stale administrative metadata, such as that left after manually deleting a worktree directory; it is not documented here as a file-recovery mechanism. [Git documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree/2.54.0.html)

## Core difference

**jsdom simulates a browser inside Node.js; Browser Mode executes tests in a real browser.** Vitest recommends Browser Mode for component testing where real browser behavior matters, while jsdom remains useful for headless tests that do not require actual rendering. [Component testing](https://vitest.dev/guide/browser/component-testing) · [Comparisons](https://vitest.dev/guide/comparisons.html)

| Aspect | jsdom | Browser Mode |
|---|---|---|
| Rendering and layout | No actual layout; layout-dependent properties such as `offsetTop` are limited. | Exercises real CSS layout and styling. |

## Presence is the key distinction

In proto3, `optional` means **track whether the field was explicitly set**, not merely “the field may be omitted.”

```proto
syntax = "proto3";
message Example {
  int32 count = 1;           // implicit presence
  optional int32 limit = 2;  // explicit presence
}
```

For `count`, the generated API cannot distinguish “never set” from “set to zero.” For `limit`, it can—even though reading either unset field returns zero. [Field Presence](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/field_presence/)

## Wire-format behavior

| State | Implicit-presence scalar | `optional` scalar |
|---|---|---|
| Unset | Not serialized | Not serialized |
| Set to default | Not serialized | Serialized |
| Set to non-default | Serialized | Serialized |

Thus, the wire format can represent an explicitly supplied default value; implicit-presence APIs simply do not retain that distinction. For example, an encoded empty string may be parsed by an implicit-presence API and then omitted when reserialized. [Field Presence](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/field_presence/)

This also means changing a field between implicit and explicit presence is binary-compatible but can lose presence information: an `optional int32` explicitly set to zero can become absent after passing through an implicit-presence client. [Field Presence](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/field_presence/)

## Defaults and generated APIs

Scalar defaults include **zero for numeric types, `false` for booleans, and empty strings/bytes**. An unset optional scalar returns its default, but its presence remains false. Explicitly assigning that same default makes presence true. [Proto3 Language Guide](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/proto3/)

Explicit-presence APIs provide presence-testing and clearing operations—conceptually `has_foo()` and `clear_foo()`, with exact spelling depending on the language. Clearing removes presence; assigning the default does not. Implicit-presence scalars generally lack presence-testing methods; the documentation notes Dart as an exception. [Field Presence](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/field_presence/)

Singular **message fields already track presence** in proto3; adding `optional` does not change their behavior. [Proto3 Language Guide](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/proto3/)

## Practical consequence

During merges, implicit-presence default values are skipped, so they cannot directly express “update this field to zero.” Explicit-presence fields merge explicitly set defaults. An implicit-presence patch protocol therefore needs an additional mechanism such as `FieldMask`. Protobuf recommends using `optional` for proto3 basic types. [Field Presence](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/field_presence/)

**Scope:** These are general protobuf semantics; language-specific accessor signatures are not detailed here.

## 1. Row-level security (RLS)

RLS is PostgreSQL’s mechanism for deciding **which rows a caller may read or modify**. Table privileges determine whether an operation is permitted at all; policies then restrict the affected rows. Enable RLS on exposed tables—once enabled, no applicable policy means no client access through the API. [RLS documentation](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security)

For example:

```sql
alter table public.todos enable row level security;

create policy "Read own todos"
on public.todos
for select
to authenticated
using ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);
```

This effectively adds a filter matching each row’s `user_id` to the signed-in user. Policies specify an operation and role:

- `USING` controls access to existing rows for reads, updates and deletes.
- `WITH CHECK` validates inserted or updated row contents.
- Updates also require a corresponding SELECT policy.

`anon` represents unauthenticated requests; `authenticated` represents signed-in users, including Supabase anonymous-auth users. Service-role credentials bypass RLS and must remain server-side. [RLS documentation](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security)

## 2. Authentication methods and configuration

Supabase Auth establishes identity; RLS determines what that identity can access. Supported methods include email/password, passwordless magic links and email OTPs, phone/SMS OTPs, social OAuth, enterprise SAML SSO, anonymous sign-in, and custom OAuth/OIDC providers. Supabase also supports selected external JWT identity providers. [Auth overview](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth)

Configuration depends on the method:

- Enable social providers through the Dashboard.
- Configure an SMS provider such as Twilio, MessageBird or Vonage for phone authentication.
- Configure allowed redirect URLs for authentication redirects.
- Optionally add TOTP or phone-based MFA. JWT assurance levels (`aal1` versus `aal2`) can be checked in RLS to require a verified second factor. [Auth overview](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth), [Users](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/users), [MFA](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/auth-mfa)

**Evidence gap:** The retrieved pages do not establish provider-specific client-ID, secret and callback-URL setup instructions; those require the relevant provider guide.

## 3. Storage access policies

Storage uses the same PostgreSQL RLS engine, with policies on **`storage.objects`**. These are separate policies: application-table rules do **not** automatically protect associated files. [Architecture guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/getting-started/the-supabase-way-to-build)

- **Private buckets** are the default; downloads require authorized access or a temporary signed URL.
- **Public buckets** allow public retrieval, but uploads, deletes, moves and copies remain access-controlled. [Bucket fundamentals](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage/buckets/fundamentals)
- Uploads require `INSERT`; overwriting with upsert additionally requires `SELECT` and `UPDATE`. Policies can constrain bucket IDs, user-specific folders or object ownership. Service keys bypass Storage RLS too. [Storage access control](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage/security/access-control)

**Bottom line:** Configure authentication, database policies and Storage policies as distinct—but identity-connected—security layers.

## 1. Row-level security (RLS)

Supabase uses PostgreSQL RLS to determine **which rows a caller can read or modify**. Table privileges determine whether a role may perform an operation; RLS policies then constrain the rows. Enable RLS and define policies explicitly:

```sql
alter table public.todos enable row level security;

create policy "Read own todos"
on public.todos for select
to authenticated
using ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);
```

This policy effectively adds a user-specific filter to queries. With RLS enabled and no applicable policies, client API access is denied. [RLS documentation](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security)

Policies specify the table, operation, role and condition:

- **`USING`** filters existing rows for SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE.
- **`WITH CHECK`** validates new rows for INSERT and resulting rows for UPDATE.
- UPDATE also needs an appropriate SELECT policy.
- `auth.uid()` supplies the caller’s user ID; `auth.jwt()` exposes JWT claims.

Unauthenticated requests use `anon`; signed-in users use `authenticated`. Service-role credentials bypass RLS and must remain server-side. [RLS documentation](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security)

## 2. Authentication methods and configuration

Supabase Auth establishes identity; RLS determines what that identity can access. Supported methods include:

- Email/password.
- Passwordless email magic links and OTPs.
- Phone/SMS OTPs.
- Social OAuth providers, such as Google, GitHub and Apple.
- Enterprise SAML SSO, custom OAuth/OIDC providers, and anonymous sign-in.

Social providers are enabled in the Dashboard. SMS authentication uses a configured messaging provider, such as Twilio, MessageBird or Vonage. Auth issues JWTs used by database and Storage authorization. [Auth overview](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth)

MFA supports TOTP authenticator apps and phone verification. Policies can require the JWT’s `aal` claim to equal `aal2`, thereby requiring a verified second factor. [MFA documentation](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/auth-mfa)

## 3. Storage access policies

Storage uses the same PostgreSQL RLS mechanism, with policies on **`storage.objects`**. These are separate from application-table policies: protecting a database record does not automatically protect its associated file. [Architecture guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/getting-started/the-supabase-way-to-build)

1. **Edit `schema.prisma`**, then run:
   ```bash
   npx prisma migrate dev --name describe_change
   ```
   Prisma replays migration history in a **shadow database** to detect drift, applies pending migrations there, generates a migration from schema changes, then applies unapplied migrations to the development database and updates **`_prisma_migrations`**. 2. **To review or customize SQL before applying it**, use:
   ```bash
   npx prisma migrate dev --create-only
   ```
   This generates a migration file without applying the new migration. Subsequently run `prisma migrate dev` to apply it. [Development migration documentation](https://docs.prisma.io/docs/cli/v7/migrate/dev)

3. **Apply committed migrations in staging/production**:
   ```bash
   npx prisma migrate deploy
   ```
   This applies pending migrations to the target database and records their applied state in `_prisma_migrations`; it does not generate new migrations. [Migration commands](https://www.prisma.io/docs/cli/v7/migrate)

| Command | Effect |
|---|---|
| `prisma migrate status` | Compares local migration history with `_prisma_migrations`; does not modify either. |

| `prisma migrate reset` | **Destructively removes data/tables** and reapplies migrations; intended for development. |
| `prisma migrate diff --script …` | Outputs SQL describing differences between schema sources; does not apply that SQL. |

Source: [Migration command documentation](https://www.prisma.io/docs/cli/v7/migrate).

- **MergeTree:** The usual choice for large datasets and high ingestion rates, particularly when you need partitioning, a sparse primary-key index, replication, or specialized merge-time processing. ## Insertion and compression

**MergeTree inserts create immutable, sorted, compressed data parts.** Compression is per column within each part; the captured quickstart identifies LZ4 as the default. Sorting similar values together improves compression, making the sorting-key choice important. [Quickstart](https://clickhouse.com/docs/get-started/quickstarts/create-your-first-mergetree-table), [reference](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/engines/table-engines/mergetree-family/mergetree)

Parts can use **Wide** storage—one file per column—or **Compact** storage—a single file for the part. The documentation recommends Compact parts for small, frequent inserts. ## Merge semantics

For **MergeTree**, background processes combine smaller parts into larger ones. **Parts from different partitions never merge.** Ordinary MergeTree merges do not inherently deduplicate rows; specialized family members add transformations—for example, replacement, summation, or aggregation. For example, **AggregatingMergeTree** combines rows with the same sorting key into aggregate-state rows during merging. Such processing is therefore distinct from simply accepting an insert. The client receives the **rendered result**, rather than executable Server Component code. ## Standard error model

A gRPC call returns a status consisting of an integer **code** and a string **message**. Success is `OK` (`0`); failure uses a predefined error code with an optional explanatory message. This model works across supported languages and does not depend on Protocol Buffers. It does **not** itself provide structured error details. [Error handling](https://grpc.io/docs/guides/error/)

## Status codes

The complete set is:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `0 OK` | Success |
| `1 CANCELLED` | Call cancelled, typically by the caller |
| `2 UNKNOWN` | Unknown or insufficiently specified error |
| `3 INVALID_ARGUMENT` | Invalid argument, regardless of system state |
| `4 DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` | Deadline expired |
| `5 NOT_FOUND` | Requested entity absent |
| `6 ALREADY_EXISTS` | Entity already exists |
| `7 PERMISSION_DENIED` | Caller lacks permission |
| `8 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` | Quota or another resource exhausted |
| `9 FAILED_PRECONDITION` | System state prevents execution |
| `10 ABORTED` | Operation aborted, often because of concurrency |
| `11 OUT_OF_RANGE` | Operation exceeds a valid range |
| `12 UNIMPLEMENTED` | Operation unsupported or not implemented |
| `13 INTERNAL` | Serious internal error or broken invariant |
| `14 UNAVAILABLE` | Service currently unavailable |
| `15 DATA_LOSS` | Unrecoverable data loss or corruption |
| `16 UNAUTHENTICATED` | Missing or invalid authentication credentials |

## At-least-once delivery

**At-least-once means a message may be delivered more than once**, rather than silently lost during a recoverable failure. Acknowledgements let the sender know that the receiver has accepted responsibility. If an acknowledgement is lost, retransmission can produce duplicates, so consumers should be **idempotent**—processing the same message again should not repeat its effects. [Reliability Guide](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/reliability)

## How consumers acknowledge messages

RabbitMQ supports two acknowledgement modes:

- **Automatic (`autoAck=true`):** RabbitMQ considers a message delivered once it is written to the socket—not once application processing succeeds. A subsequent consumer failure can lose that message.
- **Manual (`autoAck=false`):** The consumer explicitly acknowledges deliveries. For reliable processing, acknowledge **only after completing the required work**, such as recording the result in a database. RabbitMQ can then remove the message. [Acknowledgements guide](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms), [Reliability Guide](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/reliability)

With manual acknowledgements:

| Method | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `basic.ack` | Processing succeeded; RabbitMQ can discard the message. |
| `basic.reject` | Reject one delivery; optionally requeue it. |
| `basic.nack` | Reject one or multiple deliveries; optionally requeue them. |

Without requeueing, a rejected message is dead-lettered if configured, otherwise discarded. Requeueing repeatedly can create a costly redelivery loop. [Acknowledgements guide](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms)

Each delivery has a **channel-scoped delivery tag**. Acknowledge it on the **same channel** that delivered it. With `multiple=true`, an acknowledgement covers all outstanding deliveries through the specified tag; otherwise it covers only that delivery. [Acknowledgements guide](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms)

**Consumer acknowledgements travel from consumer to broker; publisher confirms travel from broker to publisher.** They protect different parts of the delivery path. pnpm uses **`pnpm-workspace.yaml` at the repository root** to define a workspace. [Workspace documentation](https://pnpm.io/workspaces)

The captured documentation describes three main categories: **package patterns, catalogs, and settings**. For example:

```yaml
packages:
  - 'packages/*'
  - 'components/**'
  - '!**/test/**'

catalog:
  chalk: ^4.1.2

catalogs:
  react16:
    react: ^16.7.0
    react-dom: ^16.7.0
```

- **`packages`** selects package directories using include/exclude glob patterns. The root package is always included.
- **`catalog`** defines the default catalog of dependency versions; **`catalogs`** defines named catalogs.
- Other top-level entries configure pnpm behavior.
- **`packageConfigs`** supplies per-project settings, either as a map or as an array of pattern-matched entries. The captured documentation says these apply per project only with `sharedWorkspaceLockfile: false`; otherwise ignored entries are reported. [Settings source](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm.io/blob/main/docs/settings.md)

## Dependency hoisting

The captured settings documentation says hoisting settings belong in **`pnpm-workspace.yaml`**, because they determine the `node_modules` structure. It identifies these controls:

| Setting | Purpose supported by captured evidence |
|---|---|
| `hoist` | Controls dependency hoisting. |
| `hoistPattern` | Selects packages to hoist using glob patterns. |
| `publicHoistPattern` | Hoists matching dependencies into top-level `node_modules`, where application code can access them. |
| `hoistWorkspacePackages` | Controls hoisting of workspace packages. |
| `shamefullyHoist` | Enables a broadly flattened, npm/Yarn-style layout for compatibility. |
| `hoistingLimits` | Limits hoisting depth. |

For example, targeted rather than broad public hoisting can be expressed as:

```yaml
packages:
  - 'packages/*'

hoistPattern:
  - '*eslint*'

publicHoistPattern:
  - '*types*'

shamefullyHoist: false
```

These fields and their placement are documented in the [settings source](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm.io/blob/main/docs/settings.md).

**Hoisting is distinct from workspace linking:** `linkWorkspacePackages` controls whether matching local packages are linked; `workspace:` dependency specifications require local resolution rather than registry fallback. [Workspace documentation](https://pnpm.io/10.x/workspaces)

## Core distinction

JSONata distinguishes **an explicit `null` value** from **an absent value**:

- **`null` is a value and a recognised data type.**
- **Absence is an empty sequence**, described as “nothing” or “no match”; it is not another spelling of `null`. [Processing model](https://docs.jsonata.org/processing)

## Paths and expressions

A path selecting a field whose value is `null` returns `null`. A path that does not exist returns nothing—represented as JavaScript `undefined`—without throwing an error. An out-of-range array index likewise returns nothing. The documentation illustrates this distinction with:

```jsonata
Other.Misc       /* null: the path exists */
Other.Nothing    /* nothing: the path does not exist */
Phone[8]         /* nothing: index out of range */
```

These examples refer to the documentation’s sample input. [Simple queries](https://docs.jsonata.org/simple)

The distinction also affects constructed output:

- An **empty sequence produces no output**.
- If an object property’s value expression produces an empty sequence, **the property is omitted**, rather than assigned `null`.
- A singleton sequence is equivalent to its sole value, so a single selected `null` remains `null`.
- Result sequences are flattened; absent subresults do not become `null` placeholders. [Processing model](https://docs.jsonata.org/processing)

## Predicates

The documented filter stage, `seq[expr]`, applies the predicate expression to each item from the preceding stage. Items that do not match are filtered out; a filter with no matches therefore produces an empty sequence, **not a `null` result or a list of `null` placeholders**. [Processing model](https://docs.jsonata.org/processing)

**Evidence limitation:** The returned source excerpts do not establish the Boolean conversion rules for `null` or an absent value used directly as a predicate, nor their exact equality/inequality semantics. Consequently, these excerpts support the presence-versus-absence and filtering rules above, but not a definitive account of expressions such as `[field]` or `[field = null]`.
