## At-least-once delivery

**At least once means a message can be delivered more than once, rather than silently lost during a recoverable failure.** RabbitMQ uses consumer acknowledgements and publisher confirms to track responsibility and support retransmission. Duplicates remain possible—for example, processing succeeds but the acknowledgement is lost. Consumers should therefore be **idempotent** or deduplicate messages. [Reliability Guide](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/reliability)

This is not an unconditional guarantee against every failure: important messages also need appropriate broker-side durability, such as durable or replicated queues and persistent messages. [Reliability Guide](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/reliability)

## How consumers acknowledge messages

In AMQP 0-9-1, consumers choose an acknowledgement mode when subscribing or fetching messages:

- **Automatic acknowledgement:** RabbitMQ considers delivery successful immediately after sending it. A consumer failure before processing can lose the message.
- **Manual acknowledgement:** The consumer sends `basic.ack` **after completing the required work**, such as committing a database update. RabbitMQ can then discard the message. [Acknowledgements Guide](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms)

Each delivery has a **delivery tag scoped to its channel**. Acknowledge it on the same channel; using another channel causes an “unknown delivery tag” error and closes that channel. With `multiple=false`, an acknowledgement covers one delivery; with `multiple=true`, it covers all outstanding deliveries up to and including that tag. Only acknowledge work that has actually completed. [Acknowledgements Guide](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms)

For unsuccessful processing:

- `basic.reject` rejects one delivery.
- `basic.nack` can reject one or multiple deliveries.
- `requeue=true` requests another delivery attempt.
- `requeue=false` sends the message to a configured dead-letter exchange, or discards it otherwise.

Unacknowledged messages are also requeued when their channel closes. Avoid immediate, endless requeue loops. [Acknowledgements Guide](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms), [Broker Semantics](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/semantics)

## Publisher confirms versus consumer acknowledgements

**Publisher confirms do not mean a consumer processed the message.** They confirm that RabbitMQ has taken responsibility for a publication; consumer acknowledgements independently confirm consumer-side processing. After a connection failure, publishers should retransmit messages whose confirms were not received—which can create duplicates if the original confirm was merely lost. [Acknowledgements Guide](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms), [Reliability Guide](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/reliability)

## What about transactions?

RabbitMQ’s AMQP transactions cover publications, acknowledgements and rejections—not database-style ACID processing. Consumption itself is not transactional, so rollback does not automatically requeue consumed messages. Even committed acknowledgements can be followed by redelivery after a server failure. **Transactions therefore do not eliminate the need for duplicate-safe consumers.** [Broker Semantics](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/semantics)

*Scope: AMQP 0-9-1; client-library API names vary.*

**Publisher confirms and transacted publishing both let a publisher know when RabbitMQ has accepted responsibility for messages, but use different mechanisms.**

| | Publisher confirms | Transacted publishing |
|---|---|---|
| **Mechanism** | RabbitMQ acknowledges publications to the publisher. The publisher tracks which messages remain unconfirmed. | Publications are grouped into an AMQP transaction; `tx.commit-ok` reports completion of the commit. |
| **Guarantee** | A confirm indicates that the broker has taken responsibility for the publication—not that a consumer processed it. | `tx.commit-ok` indicates that transaction effects are visible and the broker has accepted responsibility for publications in that transaction. |
| **After failure** | Retransmit publications whose confirms were not received. An original publication may already have succeeded, so duplicates are possible. | Do not assume database-style atomicity: RabbitMQ documents that a failure during commit can leave only some publications present, even for a single queue. |

Sources: [Consumer Acknowledgements and Publisher Confirms](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms), [Reliability Guide](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/reliability), [Broker Semantics](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/semantics).

### What neither guarantees

- **Consumer processing or exactly-once effects.** Consumer acknowledgements are separate from publisher confirms; consumers should remain duplicate-safe. [Reliability Guide](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/reliability)
- **An intended routing outcome merely from broker acceptance.** If a publisher must detect messages that cannot route to any queue, RabbitMQ documents using `mandatory` and handling `basic.return`. For transactions, returns arrive before `tx.commit-ok`. [Reliability Guide](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/reliability), [Broker Semantics](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/semantics)
- **Durability independent of configuration.** Important data still requires appropriate durable or replicated queues and persistent messages. [Reliability Guide](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/reliability)

**Practical takeaway:** confirms provide publication feedback without relying on transaction commits. Transactions group publications and acknowledgements, but should not be treated as ACID transactions.

## Workspace manifest structure

`pnpm-workspace.yaml` defines the workspace root and contains workspace membership plus pnpm settings. pnpm does **not** use the root `package.json`’s `workspaces` field for membership. The documented fields include:

- **`packages`**: a list of directory paths or glob patterns; prefix a pattern with `!` to exclude directories. The root package is always included. Current documentation says omitting `packages` includes only the root.
- **`catalog`**: a default mapping of dependency names to version ranges.
- **`catalogs`**: named mappings of dependency names to version ranges.
- **`packageConfigs`**: package-specific settings, expressed as a package-name map or an array of pattern-matched rules. Per-project resolution/layout settings require separate lockfiles (`sharedWorkspaceLockfile: false`). [Manifest reference](https://pnpm.io/pnpm-workspace_yaml)

For example:

```yaml
packages:
  - 'packages/*'
  - 'components/**'
  - '!**/test/**'

catalog:
  chalk: ^4.1.2

catalogs:
  react17:
    react: ^17.10.0
```

## Configuring dependency hoisting

These are top-level YAML settings, not children of `packages`. Current documentation places settings controlling `node_modules` structure in `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, rather than `.npmrc`. [Configuration reference](https://pnpm.io/settings)

The **pnpm 10.x reference** documents these controls:

| Setting | Documented behavior |
|---|---|
| `hoist` | Defaults to `true`; hoists dependencies into hidden `node_modules/.pnpm/node_modules`, making undeclared dependencies accessible to packages inside `node_modules`. |
| `hoistPattern` | Defaults to `['*']`; selects packages for hidden hoisting. Supports `!` exclusions. |
| `publicHoistPattern` | Defaults to `[]`; exposes matching dependencies in root `node_modules`, making undeclared dependencies accessible to application code too. Supports `!` exclusions. |
| `hoistWorkspacePackages` | Defaults to `true`; symlinks workspace packages into hidden or root `node_modules`, depending on the hoisting patterns. |
| `shamefullyHoist` | Defaults to `false`; `true` is equivalent to `publicHoistPattern: ['*']`. |

[Hoisting reference, pnpm 10.x](https://pnpm.io/10.x/settings#dependency-hoisting-settings)

A selective configuration could be:

```yaml
hoistPattern:
  - '*eslint*'
  - '*babel*'

publicHoistPattern:
  - '*plugin*'
```

Separately, **`nodeLinker: hoisted`** chooses a flat, symlink-free `node_modules` layout, unlike the default `isolated` linker. It is a layout choice, not merely a public-hoisting pattern. [Linker reference](https://pnpm.io/settings/node-modules#nodelinker)

**Evidence limitation:** Detailed hoisting defaults above were captured from the versioned 10.x documentation; the current hoisting section fell outside the permitted page excerpt, so those defaults were not independently verified for the current release.

## Null is a value; absence is no value

JSONata explicitly includes **`null` in its type system**. By contrast, a missing match is an **empty sequence**, described as “nothing” or “no match.” An empty sequence does not appear in expression output; if used as a result-object property’s value, that property is omitted. An explicit `null` is therefore not interchangeable with an absent property. [Processing model](https://docs.jsonata.org/processing)

## Existence and truthiness are different tests

- **`$exists(expr)`** returns `true` when the expression evaluates to a value, and `false` when it matches nothing—for example, a nonexistent field. Consequently, `$exists(null)` is true: null is a value, even though it is false in Boolean contexts.
- **`$boolean(null)` is `false`.** Other false-casting values include `false`, `0`, the empty string, empty arrays and empty objects. Thus, testing truthiness is not the same as testing whether a field exists. [Boolean functions](https://docs.jsonata.org/boolean-functions)

## Predicates

A Boolean predicate, `items[expr]`, evaluates `expr` relative to each candidate item: `true` keeps the item; `false` removes it. [Predicate expressions](https://docs.jsonata.org/predicate)

To test **presence, including explicit null**, use:

```jsonata
items[$exists(field)]
```

To test **absence**, use:

```jsonata
items[$not($exists(field))]
```

These follow directly from the documented `$exists()` and `$not()` rules and avoid confusing a present-but-false value with a missing field. [Boolean functions](https://docs.jsonata.org/boolean-functions)

## Defaulting: `?:` versus `??`

The operators deliberately use different criteria:

| Expression | Documented rule | Explicit `null` |
|---|---|---|
| `field ?: fallback` | Keep the left side only when its effective Boolean value is true | Uses fallback |
| `field ?? fallback` | Keep the left side when defined; use fallback only for missing/empty-sequence values | Preserves null |

The documentation defines these equivalences:

```jsonata
expr1 ?: expr2
/* equivalent to: */
expr1 ? expr1 : expr2

expr1 ?? expr2
/* equivalent to: */
$exists(expr1) ? expr1 : expr2
```

Thus, **`??` is absence-based coalescing, not null-replacement**. It also preserves defined `0`, `false`, and `''`, whereas `?:` supplies the fallback for those false-casting values. [Programming constructs](https://docs.jsonata.org/programming)

**Evidence limit:** The captured pages establish presence, Boolean conversion, output omission, and fallback behavior. They do not establish all missing-operand equality or inequality edge cases; those should not be inferred from these rules alone.

| `value ?? fallback` | Uses the fallback only when the left side is undefined/missing (an empty sequence). Explicit null is preserved because it is a defined value. |

For example, `null ?: "default"` yields `"default"`, whereas `null ?? "default"` yields `null`. These examples follow directly from the documented operator rules. [Other operators](https://docs.jsonata.org/other-operators)

## Null and absent are different

- **`null` is a value** in JSONata’s type system.
- **Absent means no value**: an unmatched expression produces an **empty sequence**, also described as `undefined` in the operator documentation. An empty sequence does not appear in output; if used as an object property’s value, that property is omitted. It is not replaced with `null`. [Processing model](https://docs.jsonata.org/processing), [Operators](https://docs.jsonata.org/other-operators)

For path expressions, if the left side of `.` produces nothing, the whole map expression produces nothing. Results from subsequent mapping are combined, with empty sequences contributing no values. [Path operators](https://docs.jsonata.org/path-operators)

## Testing presence versus truthiness

**`$exists(expr)` tests whether a value exists**, not whether it is truthy. It returns `false` for an unmatched path. Consequently, explicit `null` exists, as do `false`, `0`, and an empty string. **`$boolean(null)`**, by contrast, is `false`. [Boolean functions](https://docs.jsonata.org/boolean-functions)

Thus, to retain records whose `field` is present—even when null—use:

```jsonata
items[$exists(field)]
```

## Predicates and conditionals

A filter predicate normally retains an item only when its result casts to Boolean `true`; `null` therefore rejects the item. An absent result likewise does not supply a true condition. **Important exception:** numeric predicates select positions rather than test truthiness; arrays of integers select multiple positions. [Path operators](https://docs.jsonata.org/path-operators), [Boolean functions](https://docs.jsonata.org/boolean-functions)

The ternary conditional, `test ? yes : no`, also casts non-Boolean tests using `$boolean()`. [Operators](https://docs.jsonata.org/other-operators)

## Choosing a fallback

| Expression | Documented behavior |
|---|---|
| `field ?: fallback` | Uses the fallback for falsy values, including `null`, `false`, `0`, `''`, and `undefined`. |
| `field ?? fallback` | Uses the fallback only for absent/undefined results; preserves defined values, including `null`. |

These operators therefore distinguish **“missing”** from **“present but falsy.”** [Operators](https://docs.jsonata.org/other-operators)

**Scope:** These rules are supported by the four documentation pages reviewed; they do not establish every individual function’s handling of null or missing arguments.

## Core distinction

**`null` is a value; absence is no value.** JSONata includes `null` in its type system. A path that matches nothing produces an **empty sequence**, described as “nothing” or “no match.” Empty sequences do not appear in expression output; if an object property’s value is an empty sequence, that property is omitted. This is different from a property whose value is explicitly `null`. [Processing model](https://docs.jsonata.org/processing)

## Testing presence versus truth

- **`$exists(expr)` tests presence:** it returns `true` when the expression evaluates to a value and `false` when it matches nothing, such as a nonexistent field. Consequently, `$exists(null)` is `true`: null is present, even though it is false in a Boolean context.
- **`$boolean(expr)` tests effective truth:** `null` becomes `false`. Other false-valued inputs include `0`, `""`, empty arrays and empty objects. Thus a truth test is not a reliable presence test. [Boolean functions](https://docs.jsonata.org/boolean-functions)

## Predicates and conditionals

A predicate `[expr]` is evaluated relative to each candidate item: a Boolean `true` keeps the item, while `false` removes it. For an explicit presence filter, use, for example, `items[$exists(field)]`; this retains items whose `field` exists even when its value is `null`. [Predicates](https://docs.jsonata.org/predicate), [Boolean functions](https://docs.jsonata.org/boolean-functions)

The conditional `test ? yes : no` casts non-Boolean tests using `$boolean`. Therefore, a null-valued test selects the `no` branch. [Other operators](https://docs.jsonata.org/other-operators)

## Choosing a fallback

| Expression | Documented behavior |
|---|---|
| `value ?: fallback` | Uses the fallback for false-valued inputs, including `null`, `false`, `0`, `""`, and absence (`undefined`). |
| `value ?? fallback` | Uses the fallback **only for absence**—an undefined/empty-sequence result. A defined value, including `null`, is preserved. |

Despite its name, JSONata’s **coalescing operator is absence-only, not “null-or-missing” coalescing**. [Other operators](https://docs.jsonata.org/other-operators)

## Routing

An **Ingress** defines HTTP/HTTPS routing rules; an **Ingress controller** implements them. Creating the resource without a controller has no effect. `spec.ingressClassName` selects an IngressClass associated with a controller. [1]

The resource contains `apiVersion`, `kind`, `metadata`, and `spec`. Its rules associate an optional hostname and paths with backend Services and ports. Both hostname and path must match when a host is specified. [1]

Required `pathType` values are:
- **Exact:** case-sensitive, exact path matching.
- **Prefix:** case-sensitive matching by `/`-separated elements. `/app` matches `/app/orders`, but not `/application`.
- **ImplementationSpecific:** matching depends on the controller.

The longest matching path wins; equal-length matches prefer `Exact` over `Prefix`. Unmatched requests use the default backend, or controller-specific handling if none is configured. [1][2]

## TLS termination

Configure `spec.tls` with certificate hostnames and a `secretName`. The API defines TLS termination on port **443**, and can multiplex different hosts using **SNI**, where supported by the controller. Certificate names must match the configured TLS hosts. SNI selects TLS termination; the HTTP `Host` header selects the routing rule. [2]

This illustrative configuration routes HTTPS requests for `/app` and its subpaths to Service `web`, port 80:

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  ingressClassName: example-class
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - app.example.com
    secretName: app-tls
  rules:
  - host: app.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /app
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: web
            port:
              number: 80
```

Replace the class, hostname, and Secret with your deployment’s values. The Service must exist in the same namespace as the Ingress. TLS termination here does **not establish end-to-end encryption to the backend**; backend transport configuration must be checked separately. [2]

## Path rewriting

**Matching is not rewriting:** selecting `/app` as a prefix determines the backend; it does not itself specify removing `/app` from the forwarded URL. The standard path API defines matching and forwarding, not a rewrite field. [2]

Controllers commonly use `metadata.annotations` for additional behavior, but supported annotations differ by controller. Therefore, rewriting `/app/orders` into `/orders` requires your controller’s documented rewrite configuration—not merely `pathType: Prefix`. [1]

**Evidence gap:** the attempted tutorial fetch failed, so no specific rewrite-annotation syntax was verified. Avoid assuming annotations are portable between controllers.

Kubernetes recommends Gateway API for new development; the Ingress API remains available but is frozen. [1]

**Sources:**  
[1] [Kubernetes Ingress concepts](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/ingress/)  
[2] [Kubernetes Ingress API reference](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/service-resources/ingress-v1/)

## Ingress routing

An **Ingress** defines HTTP/HTTPS routing from outside a cluster to backend Services. An **Ingress controller** implements those rules; creating the resource alone does not expose anything. [1]

Its main fields are:

- `apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1`, `kind: Ingress`, and `metadata`.
- `spec.ingressClassName`: identifies the IngressClass to use.
- `spec.rules`: optional hostnames and paths mapped to backend Service names and ports.
- `spec.defaultBackend`: a fallback; without one, unmatched-request handling depends on the controller. [1]

Both the host, when specified, and path must match. Each path requires a `pathType`:
- **Exact:** case-sensitive exact match.
- **Prefix:** case-sensitive, slash-separated path-element match. `/shop` matches `/shop/item`, not `/shopping`.
- **ImplementationSpecific:** controller-defined matching.

The longest matching path wins; for equally matching paths, `Exact` takes precedence over `Prefix`. [1]

## TLS termination

Configure `spec.tls` with hostnames and the name of a Secret containing `tls.crt` and `tls.key`:

```yaml
spec:
  ingressClassName: example
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - shop.example.com
    secretName: shop-tls
  rules:
  - host: shop.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /shop
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: shop
            port:
              number: 80
```

The standard Ingress model supports TLS on port **443**, terminating encryption at the ingress. Traffic onward to the Service and Pods is plaintext in that model—not automatically end-to-end encrypted. The TLS hosts should match the routing hosts, and the certificate must cover those names. [1]

## Path rewriting

**Routing and rewriting are different:** a path rule selects a backend; a rewrite changes the URI forwarded to it.

Kubernetes documents controller-specific annotations and illustrates this NGINX annotation:

```yaml
metadata:
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /
```

This is **not a portable Ingress API field**. Annotation support and precise rewrite behavior depend on the controller; a `Prefix` match should not be assumed to strip the matched prefix. Check your controller’s documentation before relying on suffix preservation, regular-expression captures, or interactions between multiple paths. [1]

**Evidence limitation:** the Kubernetes-domain evidence supports the annotation example and controller-specific nature of annotations, but does not establish detailed regex-rewrite semantics.

**Current direction:** Kubernetes considers Ingress stable but frozen and recommends Gateway API for new functionality. [1]

## Static analysis

Stylelint is a CSS linter: it checks source code for errors and convention violations. Examples include unknown properties, duplicate selectors, malformed grid areas, naming-pattern violations and disallowed units. It complements, rather than replaces, a formatter such as Prettier. [Source](https://stylelint.io/)

## Rule configuration and severity

Configure rules in `stylelint.config.js`. **No rules are enabled by default**: enable them individually or extend a shared configuration such as `stylelint-config-standard`. Local settings override inherited settings. A rule accepts:

- A primary option to enable it.
- `[primaryOption, secondaryOptions]` for customization.
- `null` to disable it. [Source](https://stylelint.io/user-guide/configure/)

For example:

```js
export default {
  extends: "stylelint-config-standard",
  rules: {
    "block-no-empty": true,
    "number-max-precision": [2, { severity: "warning" }],
    "color-function-notation": ["modern", { disableFix: true }],
    "selector-class-pattern": null
  }
};
```

The per-rule `severity` secondary option accepts `"error"` (the default) or `"warning"`. Rules supporting message arguments can also accept a severity function; returning `null` falls back to `defaultSeverity`. [Source](https://stylelint.io/user-guide/configure/#severity)

For CI, `--max-warnings N` makes the CLI exit with code `2` when warnings exceed the limit. `--quiet` registers only error-level problems. [Source](https://stylelint.io/user-guide/options/)

## Automatic fixing

Run, for example:

```sh
npx stylelint "**/*.css" --fix
```

Autofix corrects problems **where possible**, not every violation. Its modes are:

- **`strict`**, the default: fixes only when there are no syntax errors.
- **`lax`**: uses a safe parser to fix as much as possible despite syntax errors.

Set `{ disableFix: true }` on a rule to retain checking without automatic corrections. With the Node.js API, corrected source is returned in `code`. [Options](https://stylelint.io/user-guide/options/#fix), [rule-level control](https://stylelint.io/user-guide/configure/#disablefix)

## Ignore mechanisms

**Within files**, disable all rules or selected rules, then re-enable them:

```css
/* stylelint-disable declaration-no-important -- Legacy override */
a { color: red !important; }
/* stylelint-enable declaration-no-important */
```

`stylelint-disable-line` and `stylelint-disable-next-line` limit suppression to one line. Descriptions follow ` -- `, with spaces on both sides. [Source](https://stylelint.io/user-guide/ignore-code/)

**Entire files** can be excluded using `.stylelintignore` with `.gitignore` syntax, `--ignore-path`, or configuration `ignoreFiles`. Use `overrides` instead when only selected rules should be disabled for particular files. [Source](https://stylelint.io/user-guide/ignore-code/)

Stylelint ignores `node_modules` by default. Suppressions can be audited using `--ignore-disables` and reporting options for needless, unscoped, invalid-scope or descriptionless disables. [Source](https://stylelint.io/user-guide/options/)

**Limitation:** core-rule compatibility with custom syntaxes is not guaranteed. [Source](https://stylelint.io/user-guide/options/#customsyntax)

## Static analysis and rule configuration

Stylelint checks stylesheet source against configured rules, reporting problems without running the styles in a browser. **No built-in rules are enabled by default**; use a shared configuration such as `stylelint-config-standard`, then customize it. Rules accept a primary option, `[primary, secondaryOptions]`, or `null` to disable them. File-specific `overrides` allow different rules for different files. [Configuration guide](https://stylelint.io/user-guide/configure/)

For example:

```json
{
  "extends": ["stylelint-config-standard"],
  "defaultSeverity": "error",
  "rules": {
    "block-no-empty": true,
    "number-max-precision": [2, { "severity": "warning" }],
    "color-function-notation": ["modern", { "disableFix": true }]
  }
}
```

### Severity

A rule’s secondary `severity` option can be `"error"` or `"warning"`; the default severity is `"error"`. Set `defaultSeverity` globally and override individual rules as needed. Severity controls reporting—not whether a rule is enabled. [Configuration guide](https://stylelint.io/user-guide/configure/)

For CI, `--max-warnings 0` makes any warning exceed the allowed limit; exceeding that limit produces CLI exit code `2`. `--quiet` suppresses warning-level problems. [Options](https://stylelint.io/user-guide/options/)

```sh
npx stylelint "**/*.css" --fix
```

- **Strict mode (default):** fixes only when there are no syntax errors.
- **Lax mode:** uses `postcss-safe-parser` to attempt fixes even with syntax errors.
- The Node.js API returns autofixed source in its `code` property.
- A rule’s `disableFix: true` prevents its automatic fixes while retaining its checks. Configuration comments can also disable a rule’s fixes. [Options](https://stylelint.io/user-guide/options/)

## Ignoring files or code

**Entire files:** use `.stylelintignore` with `.gitignore`-style patterns, interpreted relative to `process.cwd()`. Select another ignore file with `--ignore-path`, or configure `ignoreFiles`. Use `overrides` when only certain rules should change for a file subset. [Ignoring code](https://stylelint.io/user-guide/ignore-code/)


Other options report needless, descriptionless, invalid-scope, or unscoped disable comments. `node_modules` is ignored by default unless `--disable-default-ignores` is used. [Options](https://stylelint.io/user-guide/options/)

**Limit:** fixability depends on the particular rule; the general options documentation does not enumerate every fixable rule.

## Comparison

GitHub Actions distinguishes **what starts a workflow** from **how its jobs are ordered and constrained**.

| Approach | Documented behavior | Practical fit |
|---|---|---|
| **Event-triggered background work** | Configure `on`, such as `on: push`. Multiple events act as alternatives; simultaneous triggering events can produce multiple runs. Activity types and branch/path filters narrow execution. [1] | Reacting to repository changes rather than polling. |
| **Work triggered by another workflow** | Events generated with `GITHUB_TOKEN` generally do not start another workflow, preventing recursion. `workflow_dispatch` and `repository_dispatch` are exceptions. GitHub documents GitHub App tokens or personal access tokens for triggering other token-dependent events. [1] | Explicit automation handoffs; do not assume a workflow-generated push starts another run. |
| **Scheduled work** | GitHub documents scheduled time as a workflow-trigger category. However, the captured events page was truncated before its scheduling section. [2] | Periodic maintenance conceptually, but detailed scheduling configuration is not verified by this evidence. |
| **Dependent jobs within one workflow** | Define jobs under `jobs.<job_id>`. Use `needs` to wait for prerequisite jobs to succeed. Failure or skipping propagates to dependent jobs unless an appropriate condition overrides it; `if: ${{ always() }}` supports follow-up work regardless of prerequisite success. [3] | Multi-stage processing and cleanup without creating another workflow run. |

## Concurrency controls

By default, multiple jobs or workflow runs may execute concurrently. Set `concurrency` at workflow level to constrain entire runs, or `jobs.<job_id>.concurrency` to constrain individual jobs. [4]

- **Serialize, retaining only the latest pending work:** A group permits one running execution; by default, a new pending execution replaces an existing pending execution.
- **Prefer the newest execution:** Add `cancel-in-progress: true` to cancel the running execution too.
- **Queue multiple executions:** Set `queue: max` to retain up to 100 pending executions; additional ones are canceled. This cannot be combined with `cancel-in-progress: true`.
- **Scope carefully:** Group names are case-insensitive and shared across workflows in a repository. Including `${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}` helps isolate workflows and branches.

The migration guide documents these steps—not a Hive-compatibility toggle: [Migrating from Hive](https://trino.io/docs/current/appendix/from-hive.html)

| Step | What changes |
|---|---|
| Use `ARRAY[...]` and one-based indexes | Changes array construction and element numbering. Guard out-of-bounds subscripts with `IF` to avoid exceptions. |
| Use single quotes for strings and double quotes for identifiers | Replaces backtick identifier quoting; identifiers beginning with digits must be quoted. |
| Use `a \|\| b` and standard CAST types | Uses standard concatenation syntax and, notably, `VARCHAR` rather than `STRING`. |
| Cast an integer operand to `DOUBLE` | Produces floating-point rather than integer division. |
| Use a subquery or `WITH` | Makes a computed expression available for filtering in an outer query. |
| Replace `LATERAL VIEW explode()` with `CROSS JOIN UNNEST(...)` | Changes how arrays and maps are expanded into rows. |
| Write `INTERVAL '14' DAY` | Requires the keyword, a quoted value, and a singular unit. |
| Replace `datediff(end, start)` with `date_diff('day', start, end)` | Adds an explicit unit and reverses argument order. |

### 3. Data-write migration: a separate behavioral setting

`SET SESSION <catalog>.insert_existing_partitions_behavior = 'OVERWRITE'` permits inserts to overwrite existing partitions, providing behavior equivalent to Hive’s `INSERT OVERWRITE`. This changes **write behavior**, not parser strictness. The guide excludes encrypted HDFS, unpartitioned tables, and transactional tables from this overwrite support. ## Storage versus reuse

`Cache-Control` controls both **whether a response may be stored** and **when it may be reused**. These are distinct decisions. Directives are comma-separated, for example `Cache-Control: private, max-age=300`. [MDN: Cache-Control](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control)

| Directive | Effect |
|---|---|
| `no-store` | Private and shared caches must not store the response. |
| `private` | Allows storage only in a private cache, such as the user’s browser—not a shared CDN or proxy cache. |
| `public` | Allows shared-cache storage, including in circumstances that would otherwise prohibit it, such as requests containing `Authorization`. |
| `no-cache` | **Allows storage**, but requires validation with the origin before each reuse. It does not mean “do not store.” |

These distinctions are especially important for personalized responses: cookies alone do not make a response private. [MDN: Cache-Control](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control), [MDN: HTTP caching](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Caching)

## Freshness lifetime

- **`max-age=N`** specifies freshness for *N seconds after generation at the origin*, not after receipt. Time already spent in upstream caches counts: with `max-age=3600` and `Age: 600`, approximately 3,000 seconds remain.
- **`s-maxage=N`** sets freshness specifically for shared caches, overriding `max-age` and `Expires` there; private caches ignore it.
- **`Expires`** supplies an absolute expiration date. `max-age` takes precedence when both are present.
- A stale response need not be deleted: it may remain stored for later validation. Without explicit caching instructions, caches may apply heuristic freshness rules. [MDN: Cache-Control](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control), [MDN: HTTP caching](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Caching)

## Revalidation controls and headers

- **`must-revalidate`** allows reuse while fresh, but requires successful origin validation once stale; otherwise the cache returns `504` rather than serving stale content.
- **`proxy-revalidate`** applies that requirement only to shared caches.
- **`immutable`** indicates that the response will not change while fresh; it suits versioned or content-hashed resource URLs. [MDN: Cache-Control](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control)

Validation uses response validators in subsequent conditional requests:

- `ETag` → `If-None-Match`
- `Last-Modified` → `If-Modified-Since`

If unchanged, the origin returns **`304 Not Modified`**, without retransmitting the response body, enabling reuse of the stored representation. [MDN: HTTP caching](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Caching#validation)

**Caveats:** These rules do not guarantee revalidation during browser history restoration. Managed caches may also implement explicitly configured behavior outside standard HTTP caching. The captured pages were truncated; this is a core-directive summary, not an exhaustive treatment of every directive. [MDN: Cache-Control](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control), [MDN: HTTP caching](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Caching)

Once a response becomes **stale**, it can remain stored; staleness does not require deletion. The documented strategies differ in **when validation is required** and **which caches must enforce it**:

| Strategy | Behavior after becoming stale |
|---|---|
| Ordinary conditional revalidation | Ask the origin whether the stored representation is unchanged. Successful validation makes it reusable again. |
| `no-cache` | Requires origin validation **before every reuse**, even before the response becomes stale. Storage remains permitted. |
| `must-revalidate` | Allows reuse without validation while fresh, but **requires validation once stale**. If the origin cannot be reached, return `504 Gateway Timeout` rather than reuse the stale response. |
| `proxy-revalidate` | Same stale-response requirement as `must-revalidate`, but **only for shared caches**, not private browser caches. |

MDN notes that HTTP otherwise allows stale reuse in some circumstances, such as disconnection from the origin; `must-revalidate` prevents that fallback. [MDN: Cache-Control](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control)

### Two conditional-validation mechanisms

- **Modification time:** The server supplies `Last-Modified`; the cache later sends its value in `If-Modified-Since`.
- **Representation identifier:** The server supplies `ETag`; the cache later sends its value in `If-None-Match`.

For either mechanism, if the origin confirms that the representation is unchanged, it returns **`304 Not Modified`** without retransmitting the body. The cache can then reuse the stored representation with refreshed freshness information. [MDN: HTTP caching—Validation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Caching#validation)

**Important distinction:** `max-age` and `s-maxage` determine *when* freshness expires; validators determine *whether the stored representation has changed*. `immutable` concerns the period while a response remains fresh, rather than providing a stale-response revalidation strategy. [MDN: Cache-Control](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control)

- **`no-cache`**: storage is allowed, but the response must be validated with the origin before reuse. **It does not mean “do not store.”** [MDN: Cache-Control](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control)

### Freshness lifetime

- **`max-age=N`**: the response remains fresh for *N seconds after generation*, not after the browser receives it. Time already spent in another cache, indicated by `Age`, reduces the remaining freshness.
- **`s-maxage=N`**: sets freshness for shared caches only, overriding `max-age` and `Expires` there; private caches ignore it.
- **`Expires`**: specifies an absolute expiration date. `Cache-Control: max-age` takes precedence.
- Without explicit freshness instructions, caches may use **heuristic caching**; omitting `Cache-Control` does not necessarily prevent caching. [MDN: Cache-Control](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control), [MDN: HTTP caching](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Caching)

For example, `max-age=3600` with `Age: 600` leaves approximately 3,000 seconds of freshness. Freshness expiration makes a response **stale**, but does not require immediately deleting it. [MDN: HTTP caching](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Caching)

### Revalidation controls and headers

- **`must-revalidate`**: permits reuse while fresh, but requires successful validation once stale; if validation is unavailable, the cache must return an error rather than reuse the stale response.
- **`proxy-revalidate`**: the same restriction, but only for shared caches.
- **`immutable`**: declares that the response will not change during its freshness lifetime. [MDN: Cache-Control](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control)

Validation uses conditional requests:

- **`ETag` → `If-None-Match`**: compares the stored resource’s version identifier with the current version.
- **`Last-Modified` → `If-Modified-Since`**: checks whether the resource changed after the stored modification time; it is less accurate than an ETag.
- If unchanged, the server returns **`304 Not Modified`**, without a response body, allowing reuse of the stored content. [MDN: ETag](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/ETag), [MDN: Last-Modified](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Last-Modified), [MDN: HTTP caching](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Caching)

**Scope:** This covers the core directives. The bounded captures did not include detailed stale-serving extension rules. Browser history restoration can also bypass ordinary revalidation behavior. [MDN: Cache-Control](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control)

When a response becomes **stale**, it need not be deleted: the cache can validate it with the origin and reuse it if unchanged. The documented strategies differ in **when validation is required** and **how changes are detected**.

### When validation is required

| Directive | Behavior after becoming stale |
|---|---|
| `max-age=N` | Establishes when freshness expires; it does not itself impose the strict stale-reuse prohibition of `must-revalidate`. |
| `must-revalidate` | Requires successful origin validation before stale content can be reused. If validation is impossible, the cache must return `504 Gateway Timeout` rather than serve it stale. |
| `proxy-revalidate` | Applies the same requirement only to shared caches, such as proxies and CDNs. |
| `no-cache` | Requires validation before **every reuse**, even while fresh—not just after becoming stale. Storage remains allowed. |

These distinctions are documented in [MDN’s Cache-Control reference](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control).

### How validation works

- **Version-based validation:** The cached response’s `ETag` is sent in `If-None-Match`. The server compares it with the current resource’s tag. If unchanged, it returns **`304 Not Modified` without a body**, allowing the cached response to be reused. [MDN: ETag](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/ETag)
- **Time-based validation:** The cached `Last-Modified` timestamp is sent in `If-Modified-Since`. If the resource has not changed since that time, the server returns **`304 Not Modified`**, refreshing the stored response’s usability. MDN describes `Last-Modified` as less accurate than an ETag and useful as a fallback when ETags are unavailable. [MDN: HTTP caching](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Caching), [MDN: Last-Modified](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Last-Modified)

**Key distinction:** Cache directives determine **whether validation is mandatory**; validators determine **whether the stored representation still matches the origin**.

**Evidence limitation:** The captured base evidence lists `stale-while-revalidate` and `stale-if-error`, but does not contain their detailed rules. It is insufficient to compare their background-validation or stale-serving windows reliably.

HTTP caching separates **storage** (whether a response may be saved), **freshness** (how long it can be reused), and **revalidation** (checking whether the saved response is still current). `Cache-Control` supplies comma-separated directives controlling these behaviors. [1]

### Storage directives

- **`no-store`**: neither private browser caches nor shared caches should store the response.
- **`private`**: storage is allowed only in a private cache, such as the user’s browser—appropriate for personalized content.
- **`public`**: permits shared-cache storage, including responses that would otherwise be restricted because the request contains `Authorization`.
- **`no-cache` does not prohibit storage**: it permits saving the response but requires origin-server validation before each reuse. [1]

### Freshness lifetime

- **`max-age=N`**: the response remains fresh for *N seconds after generation*, not after arrival at the browser. Time already spent in upstream caches, reported through `Age`, reduces the remaining lifetime.
- **`s-maxage=N`**: specifies freshness for **shared caches only**, overriding `max-age` and `Expires` there.
- **`Expires`**: specifies an absolute expiration time. `max-age` takes precedence when both are present.
- Without explicit freshness instructions, some responses may be cached heuristically—for example, using `Last-Modified`. Omitting `Cache-Control` therefore does **not** reliably prevent caching. [1][2]

A fresh response can normally be reused without contacting the origin. Becoming stale does not automatically delete it. [1][2]

### Revalidation controls and headers

- **`must-revalidate`**: permits reuse while fresh, but requires validation once stale; if validation is impossible, the cache must not simply serve the stale response.
- **`proxy-revalidate`**: the same restriction, but only for shared caches.
- **`immutable`**: declares that the response will not change during its freshness lifetime. [1]

Conditional requests make validation efficient:

| Stored response header | Subsequent request header |
|---|---|
| `ETag: "version"` | `If-None-Match: "version"` |
| `Last-Modified: <date>` | `If-Modified-Since: <date>` |

If unchanged, the server returns **`304 Not Modified` without a response body**, allowing the cached representation to be reused and its freshness updated. [2]

For example, `Cache-Control: private, max-age=600, must-revalidate` permits browser-only storage and normal reuse for ten minutes, then requires validation. By contrast, `no-cache` requires validation on every ordinary reuse. [1]

**Caveat:** MDN notes that browser history navigation, including back/forward-cache restoration, does not necessarily trigger revalidation. Directive support and managed-cache configuration can also affect behavior. [1][2]

**Sources:**  
[1] [MDN: Cache-Control](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control)  
[2] [MDN: HTTP caching](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Caching)

Once a response becomes **stale**, it need not be deleted: revalidation can make the stored response usable again. The documented strategies differ mainly in **when validation is required** and **which validator is sent**. [1][2]

### When validation is required

- **`max-age=N` alone:** establishes when freshness ends. It does not impose the strict disconnected-cache restriction of `must-revalidate`; stale reuse can be permitted in some circumstances.
- **`max-age=N, must-revalidate`:** allows reuse without validation while fresh, but **requires successful origin validation before stale reuse**. If the cache cannot validate because it is disconnected, it must return `504 Gateway Timeout` rather than reuse the stale response.
- **`proxy-revalidate`:** imposes that same stale-response requirement **only on shared caches**, not private browser caches.
- **`no-cache`:** requires validation **before every reuse**, even while fresh. Thus, once stale, its validation requirement resembles `must-revalidate`, but it also required checks throughout the freshness period. It still permits storage.
- **`no-store`:** is not a revalidation strategy—it tells caches not to store the response. [1]

### How conditional revalidation works

| Strategy | Conditional request | Unchanged result |
|---|---|---|
| Modification-time validation | Send the stored `Last-Modified` value as `If-Modified-Since` | `304 Not Modified` |
| Entity-tag validation | Send the stored `ETag` value as `If-None-Match` | `304 Not Modified` if the tag matches |

A `304` contains no response body, avoiding another download of the representation and allowing the stored response to become fresh again. `ETag` values can represent a content hash or version; modification-time validation instead relies on timestamps, which MDN notes can be difficult to synchronize across distributed servers. [2]

**Scope and gaps:** This comparison uses the captured base evidence. The captured `Cache-Control` page lists `stale-while-revalidate` and `stale-if-error`, but its truncated content does not explain their behavior, so that evidence is insufficient to compare those strategies reliably. Also, browser history restoration may bypass revalidation even with `no-cache` or `must-revalidate`. [1]

[1] [MDN: Cache-Control](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control)  
[2] [MDN: HTTP caching](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Caching)

## What linked worktrees are

A **linked worktree** is an additional working directory attached to the same Git repository. It lets you work on multiple branches simultaneously without switching your existing checkout. Worktrees share repository data, but each has its own working files, `HEAD`, index (staging area), and administrative metadata. The original checkout is the **main worktree**. [Git documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree#_description)

## Creating one

Run these commands from an existing repository:

```bash
# Create branch "hotfix" from HEAD and check it out in ../hotfix
git worktree add ../hotfix

# Check out an existing branch in another directory
git worktree add ../release release

# Explicitly name a new branch and its starting point
git worktree add -b feature ../feature main

# Create a detached-HEAD worktree for experiments
git worktree add --detach ../experiment
```

With no branch argument, Git uses the directory’s final component as the branch name: it creates that branch from `HEAD` if absent, or checks out the existing branch if available. By default, Git refuses to check out a branch already checked out in another worktree. [Creation rules and options](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree#_commands)

## Listing and removal

```bash
git worktree list
git worktree list --porcelain -z   # Script-friendly output
git worktree remove ../hotfix
```

Listing shows the main worktree first, then linked worktrees, including their checked-out revisions, branches or detached status, and locked/prunable status.

Normal removal requires a clean worktree: no modified tracked files or untracked files. `--force` permits removal of an unclean worktree, so preserve any needed local files first. The main worktree cannot be removed with this command. [Commands](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree#_commands)

## Data retention and cleanup

- **Shared versus local data:** Linked worktrees use the same repository rather than independent clones. Their private administrative directories live under `$GIT_DIR/worktrees`; `HEAD` and the index are worktree-specific. [Details](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree#_details)
- **Manual directory deletion leaves metadata:** If you delete a worktree directory manually, its administrative files remain until automatic cleanup or `git worktree prune`. Pruning cleans stale metadata; it does not recover deleted working files. [Description and cleanup](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree#_description)
- **Temporarily unavailable storage:** Use `git worktree lock --reason "External drive" <path>` to prevent pruning when a drive or network share is unavailable. Unlock it when appropriate. [Lock command](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree#_commands)

**Retention caveat:** A worktree is not a backup. The cited documentation does not promise indefinite retention of otherwise unreferenced commits.

- **List worktrees:** `git worktree list` lists the main worktree followed by linked worktrees, showing their checked-out revisions, branches (or detached `HEAD`), and locked/prunable status.
- **Remove a linked worktree:** `git worktree remove <path>` removes it only when clean—meaning no modified tracked files and no untracked files. The main worktree cannot be removed this way.
- **Uncommitted files:** Normal removal refuses to proceed if these files exist. `git worktree remove --force <path>` overrides that protection, so commit, stash, or copy anything you need before forcing removal; otherwise local changes and untracked files can be lost.
- **If you delete the directory manually:** Its administrative metadata remains until automatic cleanup or `git worktree prune`. Pruning cleans that stale metadata, not the deleted working files.

Source: [Git’s `git-worktree` documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree), using the captured base evidence.

```bash

git worktree add ../hotfix

# Check out an existing branch in another directory
git worktree add ../release release

# Explicitly create a new branch based on main
git worktree add -b feature ../feature main

# Create a detached-HEAD worktree for experiments
git worktree add --detach ../experiment
```

For the first command, if `hotfix` already exists, Git uses it provided it is not checked out elsewhere. Git normally refuses to check out the same branch in multiple worktrees. With `-b`, the starting point defaults to the current `HEAD` if none is supplied. [Creation rules and options](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree#_commands)

## Listing and removal

```bash
git worktree list
git worktree list --porcelain -z   # Stable, machine-readable output
git worktree remove ../hotfix
```

Listing shows the main and linked worktrees, their checked-out revisions and branches, and locked or prunable status. Removal normally requires a clean worktree: no modified tracked files or untracked files. `--force` permits removal of unclean worktrees, so preserve needed changes first. The main worktree cannot be removed this way. [Commands](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree#_commands)

## Data retention and cleanup

Git stores each linked worktree’s administrative metadata under `$GIT_DIR/worktrees`. If you manually delete its working directory, that metadata remains until automatically cleaned up or explicitly pruned:

```bash
git worktree prune --dry-run
git worktree prune
```

Pruning removes stale administrative information for missing worktrees—not a backup or recovery mechanism for deleted working files. For worktrees on occasionally disconnected drives or network shares, protect their metadata from pruning with:

```bash
git worktree lock --reason "External drive" ../hotfix
```

Unlock it later with `git worktree unlock ../hotfix`. Locking also guards against normal worktree moves and removal. [Retention, pruning, and locking](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree#_description)

- **List worktrees:** `git worktree list` shows the main and linked worktrees, including their checked-out revisions, branches, and locked/prunable status.
- **Remove a linked worktree:** `git worktree remove <path>`.

**Uncommitted files:** Normal removal refuses if the worktree contains modified tracked files or untracked files. `git worktree remove --force <path>` permits removal despite those files, so commit, stash, or copy anything needed first; do not expect those working files to be retained.

If you manually delete the directory instead, Git’s administrative metadata remains until automatic cleanup or `git worktree prune`. That metadata is not a backup of your uncommitted files.
